title: Hear, O Heavens
subtitle: Isaiah 1
description: The lawsuit opens: heaven and earth are called to witness against a rebellious city.
paragraphs: The vision of Isaiah son of Amoz opens the way Amos's and Hosea's books never did, in the capital, in the court, and calling heaven and earth themselves as the witnesses. Isaiah saw it during the reigns of four kings of Judah, Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, the same long span Hosea carried, but where Hosea's pulpit was the northern kingdom, Isaiah's is Jerusalem from first verse to last. The lawsuit begins with a father's complaint: “I have raised children and brought them up, but they have rebelled against Me.” And the evidence opens with the livestock: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger, but Israel does not know; My people do not understand.” The beasts know the hand that feeds them. The children do not know the Father who raised them. In the indictment's fourth verse the book's signature name for God is sounded for the first of many times, as the thing Israel has done is stated in its plainest form: “They have forsaken the LORD; they have despised the Holy One of Israel and turned their backs on Him.” Holy One of Israel, Isaiah's name for God across the whole book, enters here as a title the nation has treated with contempt.

The people are then pictured as a single beaten body: “From the sole of your foot to the top of your head, there is no soundness”, only wounds and welts and festering sores that no one has cleansed or bandaged. The land matches the body, fields devoured by foreigners in plain sight, cities burned, and the capital itself reduced to a keeper's shelter: the Daughter of Zion abandoned like a shack in a cucumber field, like a city besieged. That Jerusalem stands at all is stated as an arithmetic of mercy: “Unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors, we would have become like Sodom, we would have resembled Gomorrah.” And then the chapter turns the Sodom name around and wears it as an address, because what comes next is not aimed at the fields or the invaders. It is aimed at the worship: “Hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom; listen to the instruction of our God, you people of Gomorrah!” The men running the sacrifices are the Sodom of the sentence.

What God says about the sacrifices is the book's first shock, and it is spoken in the first person without mediation: “What good to Me is your multitude of sacrifices?” “I am full from the burnt offerings of rams and the fat of well-fed cattle; I take no delight in the blood of bulls and lambs and goats.” The calendar itself is refused: “Bring your worthless offerings no more; your incense is detestable to Me.” New Moons, Sabbaths, convocations, all of it endured no longer, and the reason given is not liturgical but criminal: “I cannot endure iniquity in a solemn assembly.” Prayer gets the same answer as sacrifice: “When you spread out your hands in prayer, I will hide My eyes from you; even though you multiply your prayers, I will not listen. Your hands are covered with blood.” Worship performed with bloody hands is not rejected for being badly done. It is rejected for being a cover, and the God being worshiped names the cover before He names anything else.

The remedy He prescribes is not a better liturgy. It is a bath and a school: “Wash and cleanse yourselves. Remove your evil deeds from My sight. Stop doing evil!” “Learn to do right; seek justice and correct the oppressor. Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow.” The widow and the fatherless, the two people in that world with no one to pay a bribe for them, are made the syllabus of true religion in the book's first chapter, and they will keep reappearing in it to the end. Then, at the indictment's very center, the tone does what it will do across all sixty-six chapters, turning from sentence to invitation in a single breath: “Come now, let us reason together”, and the most famous exchange rate in the prophets: “Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow; though they are as red as crimson, they will become like wool.” The terms on either side of the invitation are stated flatly, with no third option offered: “If you are willing and obedient, you will eat the best of the land. But if you resist and rebel, you will be devoured by the sword.”

The chapter closes with the city itself held up and renamed by its conduct: “See how the faithful city has become a harlot! She once was full of justice; righteousness resided within her, but now only murderers!” Her silver has become dross, her wine is watered, and her rulers are the indictment in office: “Your rulers are rebels, friends of thieves. They all love bribes and chasing after rewards. They do not defend the fatherless, and the plea of the widow never comes before them.” God's answer to the dross is the refiner's answer, fire in the service of restoration: “I will restore your judges as at first, and your counselors as at the beginning. After that you will be called the City of Righteousness, the Faithful City.” Zion redeemed with justice, her repentant ones with righteousness, while rebels and sinners are shattered together and the chapter's final image returns to fire with no refiner in it: “The strong man will become tinder and his work will be a spark; both will burn together, with no one to quench the flames.” Between the invitation and that fire stands the whole book: a holy God, a harlot city, a purged and renamed remnant, and a prophet just getting started. The next movement lifts the eyes from the city's present to the mountain in its future, and it is the highest ground in the book.

title: The Mountain and the Daughters of Zion
subtitle: Isaiah 2
description: The mountain of the LORD rises over a land full of idols, and the daughters of Zion parade through judgment.
paragraphs: Chapter two opens with the destination before it names the disaster, the book's habit from here on: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the LORD will be established as the chief of the mountains; it will be raised above the hills, and all nations will stream to it.” The peoples of the earth are pictured on the road uphill, saying to each other: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob. He will teach us His ways so that we may walk in His paths.” And the fruit of the teaching is the most quoted disarmament in the prophets: “They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will no longer take up the sword against nation, nor train anymore for war.” The word goes out from Jerusalem to the nations, and the chapter turns the invitation on its own audience first: “Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the LORD.” Everything that follows in the chapter is the distance between that road and the one Jacob's house is actually walking.

The present tense is an inventory of fullness that has replaced trust: “Their land is full of silver and gold, with no limit to their treasures”, full of horses and chariots, and “full of idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to what their fingers have made”. Against all of it stands the Day of the LORD, a day with one target stated a dozen ways, loftiness: cedars of Lebanon, oaks of Bashan, tall mountains, high towers, fortified walls, ships of Tarshish, everything lifted up, until the refrain arrives: “The proud look of man will be humbled, and the loftiness of men brought low; the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.” Men will flee to caves and holes from the splendor of that majesty, and on the way they will dispose of the gods they made: in that day “men will cast away to the moles and bats their idols of silver and gold”. The chapter's advice lands like a shrug at human greatness: put no more trust in man, who has only breath in his nostrils.

Chapter three makes the judgment administrative. God removes from Jerusalem and Judah “the whole supply of food and water”, and with the bread goes the entire leadership class, mighty man and warrior, judge and prophet, counselor and elder, until the vacuum is filled by whoever can be seized: “I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them.” The book illustrates the collapse with a street scene, played straight: a man grabs his brother by the cloak and offers him the rubble to rule, and the brother refuses the throne on the grounds that he has no food or clothing in his own house. Over the whole failure stands the charge against the elders, delivered in court: “You have devoured the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses.” “Why do you crush My people and grind the faces of the poor?” Vineyard language again; Hosea's nation was a wife, Amos's a field under a plumb line, and Isaiah's rulers are tenants eating the vineyard they were hired to keep.

Then the camera turns to the daughters of Zion, whose parade through the chapter is the book's portrait of a society decorating itself over a rot: heads high, eyes wanton, steps mincing, anklets jingling. The text lists their finery with a clerk's patience, crescents and pendants, bracelets and veils, headdresses and sashes, perfume bottles, mirrors, tiaras and shawls, twenty-one items of ornament itemized only so the exchange can be stated in the same currency: “Instead of fragrance there will be a stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of styled hair, baldness; instead of fine clothing, sackcloth; instead of beauty, shame.” The men fall by the sword, the gates of Zion sit destitute on the ground and mourn, and the chapter of ornaments ends with seven women taking hold of one man, offering to feed and clothe themselves if only his name will take away their disgrace. Nothing in the first movement is colder than that arithmetic of survival.

Chapter four answers it in six verses, the shortest chapter so far and the hinge of the whole book's hope. “On that day the Branch of the LORD will be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land will be the pride and glory of Israel’s survivors.” Branch is a name the book will grow; here it stands simply as the glory restored to a remnant recorded among the living, and the survivors' holiness is tied to a washing: holy is whoever remains in Zion “when the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains from the heart of Jerusalem by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of fire”. The filth of the ornamented daughters and the bloodstains of the bloody-handed city are both washed in the same verse. And over the cleansed mountain God recreates the exodus sky, pillar and canopy at once: “For over all the glory there will be a canopy”, “a shelter to give shade from the heat by day, and a refuge and hiding place from the storm and the rain”. The movement that began on the mountain of the nations ends under a canopy over a washed city. The next sound in the book is a love song, and it is going to end like a lawsuit.

title: The Song of the Vineyard
subtitle: Isaiah 5
description: A love song for a vineyard turns into six woes, and fire answers the diagnosis.
paragraphs: The book's third sound, after lawsuit and vision, is a love song, and it opens in the voice of a friend: “I will sing for my beloved a song of his vineyard”. It is sung about the friend's vineyard on a fertile hill. Everything a vintner can do has been done in the telling: the ground dug up, the stones cleared, the finest vines planted, a watchtower built in the middle, a winepress cut into the rock. The care is exhaustive and the result is a single devastating sentence: “He waited for the vineyard to yield good grapes, but the fruit it produced was sour!” Then the singer steps out from behind the song and hands the case to the audience: “And now, O dwellers of Jerusalem and men of Judah, I exhort you to judge between Me and My vineyard.” “What more could have been done for My vineyard than I have done for it? Why, when I expected sweet grapes, did it bring forth sour fruit?” The jury is asked to acquit the gardener. There is nothing left to argue.

The sentence follows: “Now I will tell you what I am about to do to My vineyard: I will take away its hedge, and it will be consumed; I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled.” No pruning, no rain, briers and thorns unopposed. And only then does the song name its subject, in the verse the whole parable exists to deliver: “For the vineyard of the LORD of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are the plant of His delight. He looked for justice, but saw bloodshed; for righteousness, but heard a cry of distress.” In the Hebrew the two pairs nearly rhyme, justice and bloodshed, righteousness and a cry, the expected sound and the sound that came. The vineyard figure will follow this book to its last chapters, and it follows the series too: Hosea's Israel was a luxuriant vine building altars out of its fruitfulness; Isaiah's is a tended garden producing the opposite of its planting. The rest of the chapter is the evidence read aloud, six woes that itemize the sour grapes.

The first two woes are the economics and the anesthesia of the ruling class. Land: “Woe to you who add house to house and join field to field until no place is left and you live alone in the land.” The sentence matches the sin in kind, mansions emptied for the men who emptied everyone else: “Surely many houses will become desolate, great mansions left unoccupied.” Drink: “Woe to those who rise early in the morning in pursuit of strong drink, who linger into the evening, to be inflamed by wine.” Their feasts are fully equipped, lyre and harp and tambourine and flute, everything except attention: “They disregard the actions of the LORD and fail to see the work of His hands.” The consequence of not seeing is named in advance and it is the movement's first exile sentence: “Therefore My people will go into exile for their lack of understanding”, dignitaries starving, the masses parched, and below them all the appetite that swallows a society whole: “Therefore Sheol enlarges its throat and opens wide its enormous jaws”. “So mankind will be brought low, and each man humbled; the arrogant will lower their eyes.”

The remaining woes go inward, to the conscience and the courts. Men dragging their sins behind them like freight: “Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of deceit and pull sin along with cart ropes”, daring God to perform on schedule: “Let Him hurry and hasten His work so that we may see it!” Then the woe the centuries have never improved on, the vocabulary of a society that has lost its nouns: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who turn darkness to light and light to darkness, who replace bitter with sweet and sweet with bitter.” “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and clever in their own sight.” And the legal system sold: “Woe to those who are heroes in drinking wine and champions in mixing strong drink”, the men “who acquit the guilty for a bribe and deprive the innocent of justice”. The root diagnosis under all six is a refusal of the book itself: “they have rejected the instruction of the LORD of Hosts and despised the word of the Holy One of Israel”.

Fire answers the diagnosis, straw and dry grass language, roots decaying and blossoms blowing away like dust, and then the refrain that will toll through the next four chapters like a bell over Israel: “Therefore the anger of the LORD burns against His people; His hand is raised against them to strike them down.” “Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.” Despite all this. The woes were not the end of the anger; they were barely its beginning. The chapter closes by looking past Judah to the instrument being summoned from the horizon, described with a scout's admiration and a victim's dread: “He lifts a banner for the distant nations and whistles for those at the ends of the earth.” An army that never sleeps, whose sandal straps do not break, whose arrows are sharpened and chariot wheels are a whirlwind, coming to roar over the vineyard like the sea. The song has become an invasion notice. Before the invasion arrives, the book stops and goes back to a throne room, in the year a king died, to show how the singer himself was made.

title: In the Year Uzziah Died
subtitle: Isaiah 6
description: In the year Uzziah died, Isaiah sees the King, is cleansed by a coal, and meets the first sign-child.
paragraphs: The book's commissioning vision is dated by a death: “In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated on a throne, high and exalted; and the train of His robe filled the temple.” Uzziah had reigned fifty-two years; the throne of Judah stood empty, and Isaiah's sight is deliberately filled with the throne that is not. Above it stand the seraphim, six-winged, two wings for their faces, two for their feet, two for flight, calling the trisagion that gives the book its God-name its music: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts; all the earth is full of His glory.” The doorposts shake, the temple fills with smoke, and the prophet's response is the only honest one available to him, because the vision's first effect is not empowerment but exposure: “Woe is me, for I am ruined, because I am a man of unclean lips dwelling among a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of Hosts.” Lips, the prophet's instrument, are the named ruin. He does not confess Judah's sins. He confesses that his own mouth belongs to the indicted people.

The remedy comes from the altar, carried in tongs: a glowing coal touches the very organ condemned, and the words spoken over it are the book's gospel in advance: “Now that this has touched your lips, your iniquity is removed and your sin is atoned for.” Then the question that has been waiting for a cleansed volunteer: “Whom shall I send? Who will go for Us?” And the answer the whole book depends on: “Here am I. Send me!” What he is sent to say is the strangest commission in the prophets, a preaching assignment described in terms of its failure: “Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving.” “Make the hearts of this people calloused; deafen their ears and close their eyes. Otherwise they might see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their hearts, and turn and be healed.” The word will harden the hearers who refuse it; the prophet's question is the only one left, “How long, O Lord?” and the answer is measured in ruins, cities without inhabitant, land utterly forsaken, a tenth burned again after the burning. The vision ends on the book's first stump: “As the terebinth and oak leave stumps when felled, so the holy seed will be a stump in the land.” A felled tree as a seed. The series has followed stumps before; Isaiah's book will spend sixty chapters growing this one.

The first errand shows the prophet at work, and God sends him out with one of his children, because in this book even the family is a placard. The crisis is the Syro-Ephraimite war: Aram and the northern kingdom have marched on Jerusalem to force Judah into their alliance against Assyria and install a puppet, and the hearts of King Ahaz and his people are shaking like trees in a wind. God sends Isaiah and his son Shear-jashub, whose name means A Remnant Will Return, to meet the king at the aqueduct of the upper pool, where Ahaz is inspecting his water supply for the siege. The message is almost insultingly calm: “Calm down and be quiet. Do not be afraid or disheartened over these two smoldering stubs of firewood”, the two allied kings demoted to smoking stick-ends. “It will not arise; it will not happen.” Within sixty-five years Ephraim will be shattered as a people; the alliance has an expiry date the allies do not know about. The condition put to Ahaz is the book's thesis for kings, stated as a wordplay on standing: “If you do not stand firm in your faith, then you will not stand at all.”

Then God offers the shaken king the one thing frightened kings are not usually offered, a blank check of proof: “Ask for a sign from the LORD your God, whether from the depths of Sheol or the heights of heaven.” Ahaz refuses, and dresses the refusal as piety: “I will not ask; I will not test the LORD.” Isaiah's patience ends in the hearing: “Hear now, O house of David! Is it not enough to try the patience of men? Will you try the patience of my God as well?” The sign is therefore given to the house, over the king's head and against his timetable: “Therefore the Lord Himself will give you a sign: Behold, the virgin will be with child and give birth to a son, and will call Him Immanuel.” Immanuel, God With Us, and the oracle itself keeps the sign inside the crisis it was given for, tying it to the boy's own childhood as the measure of the alliance's end: “For before the boy knows enough to reject evil and choose good, the land of the two kings you dread will be laid waste.” The sign's comfort and its threat are the same child, because the God who is with us is also bringing the flood Ahaz's unbelief is choosing: “The LORD will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father a time unlike any since the day Ephraim separated from Judah”, and the sentence ends by naming the flood's name for the first time in the book's narrative, the king of Assyria, hired like a razor from beyond the Euphrates to shave the land bare. The king who would not ask has been answered anyway. The next movement stays with the prophet's children, the flood already rising in the words.

title: God Is With Us
subtitle: Isaiah 8
description: A second sign-child, a flood Judah chose, a stone to stumble on, and then a great light and a child.
paragraphs: The book's second placard child arrives by paperwork before he arrives by birth. God tells Isaiah: “Take a large scroll and write on it with an ordinary stylus: Maher-shalal-hash-baz.” Ordinary stylus, characters anyone could read, witnesses appointed, Uriah the priest and Zechariah, so the prediction would be a matter of public record before it happened. Then the prophetess conceives, and the name is given to the boy in the cradle: Maher-shalal-hash-baz, Speeding to the Plunder, Quick to the Spoil. His milestones are the prophecy's clock: “For before the boy knows how to cry ‘Father’ or ‘Mother,’ the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria.” Before this child can talk, the two smoldering stubs of chapter seven will be plundered by the very empire Ahaz is courting. Isaiah's nursery is a war room; his sons' names are headlines, one promising a remnant's return, one timing an invasion, and the child between them, Immanuel, naming the God who oversees both.

The oracle explains the flood in water language. Judah has refused one water supply and will be given another: “this people has rejected the gently flowing waters of Shiloah”, the quiet channel that fed Jerusalem from the Gihon spring, soft water for a city that would not trust softly. The replacement is the Euphrates at flood stage: “the Lord will surely bring against them the mighty floodwaters of the Euphrates”, Assyria and all his pomp, rising through Israel and into Judah itself: “It will pour into Judah, swirling and sweeping over it, reaching up to the neck; its spreading streams will cover your entire land, O Immanuel!” Up to the neck, and no further in the picture; the head stays above water, and the land under the flood is still addressed by the child's name, Immanuel's land. Against the nations massing in the same oracle, the name becomes a defiance: “Devise a plan, but it will be thwarted; state a proposal, but it will not happen. For God is with us.” God is with us is the literal meaning of the name Ahaz refused to ask for, now preached as a war cry over the flood.

Isaiah's own instructions in the crisis are a discipline of fear. He is told not to call conspiracy what the panicking city calls conspiracy, not to fear what it fears: “The LORD of Hosts is the One you shall regard as holy. Only He should be feared; only He should be dreaded.” The God so regarded makes the strangest promise of the chapter, sanctuary and stumbling in the same person: “He will be a sanctuary”, and to both houses of Israel “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense”, a trap and a snare for Jerusalem's dwellers, over whom many will fall and be broken. Then the prophet withdraws from the public square into the posture he will hold for the rest of the book: the testimony bound up and sealed among his disciples, the waiting begun: “I will wait for the LORD, who is hiding His face from the house of Jacob. I will put my trust in Him.” And the family stands as its own exhibit: “Here am I, and the children the LORD has given me as signs and symbols in Israel from the LORD of Hosts, who dwells on Mount Zion.” When the terrified people run to mediums and spiritists who whisper and mutter, the book's rule is pronounced over the whole consultation industry: “To the law and to the testimony! If they do not speak according to this word, they have no light of dawn.”

The chapter of darkness ends with the hungry cursing their king and their God and being driven into utter gloom, and chapter nine opens on the very districts the flood reached first, Zebulun and Naphtali, the northern lands humbled first and honored first in the reversal: “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light; on those living in the land of the shadow of death, a light has dawned.” The joy is described in harvest and plunder terms, and its mechanics are Midian's: “For as in the day of Midian You have shattered the yoke of their burden, the bar across their shoulders, and the rod of their oppressor.” Gideon's day, when the battle was won without Israel's strength, is the template, and the boots and blood-rolled garments of war are fuel for a fire. Then comes the announcement the whole movement has been carrying since the aqueduct, the child of the sign now enthroned in the oracle: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given, and the government will be upon His shoulders. And He will be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace.” “Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end. He will reign on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and sustain it with justice and righteousness from that time and forevermore. The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.” In this book the oracle stands in its own place, between the flood of Assyria and the refrain of anger, given to a people whose present king would not ask for it.

For the refrain comes back at once, over Ephraim's pride in its own ruins: “The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with finished stone; the sycamores have been felled, but we will replace them with cedars.” Rebuilding as defiance, answered by enemies raised and a land devoured with open mouths: “Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.” It sounds three times in the chapter, over the people who did not return to Him who struck them, over the leaders who mislead and the guided who are swallowed, over the fire of wickedness in which brother devours brother, Manasseh Ephraim and Ephraim Manasseh and both against Judah. And it will sound once more in the next episode, over the decree-writers of Judah themselves, before the book finally turns the refrain on the rod in God's own hand.

title: The Rod of My Anger
subtitle: Isaiah 10
description: Assyria is the rod in God's hand, and the rod does not know it.
paragraphs: Chapter ten opens where chapter five's woes left off, with the last stroke of the refrain reserved for Judah's own lawmakers: “Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees, to deprive the poor of fair treatment and withhold justice from the oppressed of My people, to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder.” The widow and the orphan, chapter one's syllabus, are here the prey of the statute book itself; injustice in Isaiah is not only committed, it is legislated. The day of reckoning is put to them as three unanswerable questions: “What will you do on the day of reckoning when devastation comes from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth?” Nothing remains but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain, and the bell tolls its fourth and final time over this movement: “Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised.” Then, in the same breath, the book turns the woe on the instrument of the anger itself, and the whole theology of the Assyrian crisis is stated in one address: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger; the staff in their hands is My wrath.”

The rod, it turns out, has intentions. God sends Assyria against a godless nation to take spoil and trample like clay in the streets; the king's own heart keeps a different ledger: “But this is not his intention; this is not his plan. For it is in his heart to destroy and cut off many nations.” The instrument does not know it is an instrument, and its ignorance is quoted at length, the conqueror's arithmetic of fallen capitals, Calno like Carchemish, Hamath like Arpad, Samaria like Damascus, and Jerusalem next in the sequence. His conquest speech is allowed to run to its most vivid image on its own terms: “By the strength of my hand I have done this, and by my wisdom, for I am clever.” “Like one gathering abandoned eggs, I gathered all the earth. No wing fluttered, no beak opened or chirped.” The world as a nest of unguarded eggs, gathered without a sound. God's answer is not a rebuttal of the facts. The conquests are real. The answer is a category question, the book's most famous reductio: “Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it? Does a saw boast over him who saws with it?” A rod waving the one who lifts it, a staff lifting him who is not wood: the image itself is the verdict, and the wasting disease promised among Assyria's stout warriors, the fire kindled under his pomp, follows like a footnote.

The forest arithmetic is then done on the empire: the Light of Israel becomes a fire, forests and orchards destroyed soul and body in a single day, until “The remaining trees of its forests will be so few that a child could count them.” And against that emptied forest, the chapter sets the doctrine the whole movement has been naming in a child's name since the aqueduct. Shear-jashub stood beside his father at the upper pool; here his name is preached: “A remnant will return”, in the text's own words “a remnant of Jacob”, “to the Mighty God”. The promise is deliberately narrowed past comfort into something harder: “Though your people, O Israel, be like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return.” Sand of the sea is the patriarchal promise's own measure, and the book does not flinch from the fraction: the return will be real, and it will be a remnant, destruction decreed and overflowing with righteousness in the same decree. Zion's part in it is an instruction against fear, addressed to the city that watched the flood reach its neck: “O My people who dwell in Zion, do not fear Assyria, who strikes you with a rod and lifts his staff against you as the Egyptians did.” In a little while the fury subsides and turns, whip and staff raised against Assyria as once against Midian and Egypt.

The chapter closes with the invasion itinerary read like a dispatch, town by town, the army's approach march narrated in present tense until it stands at the last ridge: Aiath, Migron, Michmash, the ford at Geba, Ramah trembling, Gibeah of Saul in flight, Gallim crying aloud, poor Anathoth, Madmenah fleeing, and the army halting at Nob, close enough to see the city, “shaking a fist at the mount of Daughter Zion, at the hill of Jerusalem”. One ridge from Jerusalem, and the fist is the last thing the chapter shows of Assyria's strength, because the answer is a forestry sentence spoken over the empire that counted other nations' trees: “Behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts will lop off the branches with terrifying power. The tall trees will be cut down, the lofty ones will be felled.” Lebanon itself falls before the Mighty One. A felled forest, and in the book's stump theology that is not the end of a tree. The next episode opens at exactly that spot, at a stump in David's line, with something already growing out of it.

title: The Shoot of Jesse
subtitle: Isaiah 11
description: From Jesse's stump, a shoot; from the shoot, a world at peace and a second exodus.
paragraphs: The vision of chapter six ended with a stump, and the forestry of chapter ten ended with a felled Lebanon, and chapter eleven opens at the exact spot where both left off, only now the stump belongs to a named family: “Then a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse, and a Branch from his roots will bear fruit.” Jesse, David's father, the root of the royal house now reduced in Isaiah's day to a dynasty of Ahazes; the book does not say throne or crown, it says stump, a thing cut down to ground level, and out of the cut surface, a shoot. The Branch name sounded once already, beautiful and glorious in chapter four, and here its endowment is listed as carefully as the daughters' finery was: “The Spirit of the LORD will rest on Him”, and the Spirit is named in His fullness, “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and fear of the LORD”. His delight is in the fear of the LORD, and His courtroom reverses every court in the book: “He will not judge by what His eyes see, and He will not decide by what His ears hear, but with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth.” The poor and the lowly, the ground-down faces of chapter three, get a judge who does not need the bribe or the dossier: “He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips.”

Then the stump's orchard becomes the world's peace, in the passage no retelling of Isaiah is permitted to rush: “The wolf will live with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the goat; the calf and young lion and fatling will be together, and a little child will lead them.” Cow and bear grazing together, the lion eating straw like the ox, and the most dangerous real estate in creation made a nursery: “The infant will play by the cobra’s den, and the toddler will reach into the viper’s nest.” The condition under the whole scene is stated as its ground, and it is chapter one's missing quantity finally supplied to the whole earth: “They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the sea is full of water.” Knowledge of God, whose absence opened the book's lawsuit and destroyed Hosea's people, is here the climate of the world, as total as water in the sea. Nor is the shoot a private king for a private people: “On that day the Root of Jesse will stand as a banner for the peoples. The nations will seek Him, and His place of rest will be glorious.” Root and shoot in one figure, Jesse's descendant and Jesse's source, a banner the nations themselves come looking for.

The gathering follows, and it is described as an exodus done a second time, the Lord extending “His hand a second time to recover the remnant of His people” from the full compass of the dispersion, Assyria, Egypt, Pathros, Cush, Elam, Shinar, Hamath, and the islands of the sea. The old fratricide is retired inside the promise: Ephraim's jealousy departs, Judah stops harassing Ephraim, and the reconciled brothers plunder their old enemies together. The geography of the first exodus is rerun with variations, the gulf of the Sea of Egypt devoted to destruction, the Euphrates split into seven streams for sandaled feet, and the movement's whole road system summarized in one verse: “There will be a highway for the remnant of His people who remain from Assyria, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.” Highway is a word this book will keep building with until its last chapters; the road home is under construction from here on.

Chapter twelve is six verses long and is given whole, because the book gives it as the song the delivered people will sing, and a song quoted in fragments is not a song. It begins in the first person, in that day you will say: “O LORD, I will praise You. Although You were angry with me, Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me.” The anger admitted, the turning celebrated, and then the confession that answers the aqueduct, where a king would not stand firm in faith: “Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation.” Salvation, salvation, salvation, three times in two verses, and water again for the drawing: “With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation”, Shiloah's gentle waters become wells for the whole delivered people. The song turns outward in its second half, from confession to proclamation: “Give praise to the LORD; proclaim His name! Make His works known among the peoples; declare that His name is exalted.” The peoples, who in chapter two stream up the mountain to be taught, are here told the works by the people who lived them. And the song lands where the whole first movement has been aiming since the vineyard went sour: “Sing to the LORD, for He has done glorious things. Let this be known in all the earth.” “Cry out and sing, O citizen of Zion, for great among you is the Holy One of Israel.” Great among you. The despised title of chapter one is now the resident glory of the city, and the first twelve chapters close with the city's citizen singing, before the burdens turn outward to the nations who have so far only been promised a road in.

title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon
subtitle: Isaiah 13
description: The burdens open: Babylon falls, its king is taunted in Sheol, and God's purpose stands over the whole earth.
paragraphs: The burdens against the nations open with the empire that has not yet arrived. In Isaiah's lifetime Babylon is a city inside the Assyrian world, not its master; the book's first burden is against her anyway, received as a vision of her end: a banner on a barren hilltop, an army mobilized from the ends of heaven, and the sound of the Day of the LORD approaching as a weather event: “Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near; it will come as destruction from the Almighty.” Hands fall limp, hearts melt, labor pains seize a city of conquerors, and the day itself is defined in the fragment the dashes allow: “Behold, the Day of the LORD is coming”, “cruel, with fury and burning anger”, to make the earth a desolation. The sky is conscripted into the judgment: “For the stars of heaven and their constellations will not give their light. The rising sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light.” And the purpose is the book's steady one, against loftiness wherever it sits: “I will punish the world for its evil and the wicked for their iniquity. I will end the haughtiness of the arrogant and lay low the pride of the ruthless.” Man scarcer than gold, the heavens trembling, the hunted fleeing home to die there anyway; the Medes stirred up as the instrument, with no regard for silver or gold, and their work stated in the text's own terms, as the outline promised, neither elaborated nor looked away from: “Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes, their houses will be looted, and their wives will be ravished.”

The city's epitaph is written in Sodom's grammar: “And Babylon, the jewel of the kingdoms, the glory of the pride of the Chaldeans, will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah.” “She will never be inhabited or settled from generation to generation”, no nomad's tent, no shepherd's flock, only desert creatures in the luxurious palaces and hyenas in the fortresses. And then the burden turns before it ends, because Isaiah's Babylon exists in the book chiefly as the backdrop for Israel's rest: the LORD will have compassion on Jacob, choose Israel again, settle them in their own land, and on the day of rest the captives get a song to sing at their captor. It is introduced as what it is: “you will sing this song of contempt against the king of Babylon: How the oppressor has ceased, and how his fury has ended!” The staff of the wicked is broken, the scepter snapped, and the whole earth, so recently the king's highway of conquest, is at peace and at rest and breaking into song. Even the timber celebrates: the cypresses and cedars of Lebanon, spared at last, exult over the fallen woodcutter, “Since you have been laid low, no woodcutter comes against us.”

The taunt then follows the king down, and Sheol itself is pictured as a court rising for an unwelcome guest of honor: the grave beneath is eager to meet him, stirring the spirits of dead kings from their thrones to deliver the welcome in chorus: “You too have become weak, as we are; you have become like us!” The harps go down with him: “Your pomp has been brought down to Sheol, along with the music of your harps. Maggots are your bed and worms your blanket.” And in that setting the book speaks its most analyzed sentence, addressed by the text to this king in his fall, in the words the BSB gives them: “How you have fallen from heaven, O day star, son of the dawn! You have been cut down to the ground, O destroyer of nations.” The heart that produced the fall is quoted in its own first person, five ascents in two verses: “I will ascend to the heavens; I will raise my throne above the stars of God.” “I will ascend above the tops of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.” The answer is a single reversal of direction: “But you will be brought down to Sheol, to the lowest depths of the Pit.” The onlookers at the pit's edge perform the world's final audit of empire, staring and wondering: “Is this the man who shook the earth and made the kingdoms tremble”, the man who turned the world into a desert and would not let his captives go home, now cast out of burial itself like a rejected branch, denied even the tomb every other king in the song is lying in state inside.

The episode closes by widening from Babylon to the near horizon and then to the whole earth. The God who speaks the taunt binds Himself to it with an oath: “Surely, as I have planned, so will it be; as I have purposed, so will it stand.” Assyria, the present terror standing over Isaiah's own audience, is folded into the same purpose and scheduled for the same ground: “I will break Assyria in My land; I will trample him on My mountain.” His yoke comes off, his burden lifts from shoulders, and the plan is declared to be not a local arrangement but a design for the whole earth, a hand stretched out over all the nations that no one can turn back. A short Philistia burden, dated to the year King Ahaz died, seals the movement's opening: do not rejoice that the rod that struck you is broken, for a worse snake is hatching from the same root, a cloud of smoke coming from the north with no stragglers in its ranks. And when the envoys of that frightened nation come asking for an answer, the answer the book files is the one its whole burden section exists to give: “The LORD has founded Zion, where His afflicted people will find refuge.”

title: My Heart Cries Out for Moab
subtitle: Isaiah 15
description: The prophet weeps over Moab, Damascus and Ephraim fade together, and gifts come up from Cush.
paragraphs: The Moab burden is the strangest of the oracles, because the prophet cannot stop grieving the nation he is sentencing. It begins with speed, two cities gone in a single night: “Ar in Moab is ruined, destroyed in a night! Kir in Moab is devastated, destroyed in a night!” Dibon goes up to its temple to weep, heads shaved, beards cut, sackcloth in the streets, the whole country wailing on rooftops and in squares, its soldiers' souls trembling inside them. And into the national lament a first-person voice keeps breaking, unmistakably the prophet's own: “My heart cries out over Moab”. His heart cries out, and later it does more than cry: “So I weep with Jazer for the vines of Sibmah; I drench Heshbon and Elealeh with my tears.” “Therefore my heart laments for Moab like a harp, my inmost being for Kir-heres.” No other burden in the book is carried this way; the judge is in tears over the dock, and the text does not treat the tears as a contradiction of the sentence. The sentence runs its course regardless: fugitives as far as Zoar, waters of Nimrim dried, wealth carried over the Brook of the Willows, the waters of Dimon full of blood with more promised, a lion for the fugitives who escape the first ruin.

What Moab is counseled to do, in the oracle's middle, is remarkable enough to quote carefully: send tribute lambs to the ruler of the land, to the mount of Daughter Zion; shelter the fugitives at noonday, hide the refugees, do not betray the one who flees; let Moab's outcasts stay with you, and the pronouns shift until Zion is being asked to be the refuge Moab never was. And inside Moab's own oracle stands a throne promise that belongs to the great arc of the book: “in loving devotion a throne will be established in the tent of David. A judge seeking justice and hastening righteousness will sit on it in faithfulness.” David's tent, the stump of Jesse again, promised in a paragraph addressed to a dying neighbor. But Moab's pride is the diagnosis the book returns to: pomposity, exceeding pride, overflowing arrogance, empty boasting. The raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth are mourned, the cheering is ended in the winepresses, Moab wears himself out at his high place and enters his sanctuary to pray and it does him no good, and the timetable is given in a hired worker's precision: “In three years, as a hired worker counts the years, Moab’s splendor will become an object of contempt”, and those left will be few and feeble.

Damascus follows, and the burden against Aram cannot be told without Ephraim inside it, because the two were allies in the war that opened this book: “Behold, Damascus is no longer a city; it has become a heap of ruins.” The fortress disappears from Ephraim, the sovereignty from Damascus, and Jacob's splendor fades to a reaper's leavings: “Yet gleanings will remain, like an olive tree that has been beaten”, two or three berries at the top, four or five on the fruitful branches, the remnant doctrine translated into harvest language. And the gleanings produce the book's quiet miracle in the middle of a ruin oracle: “In that day men will look to their Maker and turn their eyes to the Holy One of Israel.” They will not look to the altars their hands fashioned, because the disease has been diagnosed at last: “For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and failed to remember the Rock of your refuge.” The nations raging around them are disposed of in weather: rebuked, they flee like chaff on the hills and tumbleweeds before a gale; in the evening, sudden terror, and before morning, they are no more.

The movement's last picture is the farthest south the burdens reach, the land of whirring wings beyond the rivers of Cush, tall and smooth-skinned messengers in papyrus boats, a feared nation of strange speech sending envoys to Zion. The answer they receive is a portrait of God as the calmest actor in the book: “I will quietly look on from My dwelling place, like shimmering heat in the sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.” No panic, no hurry; before the harvest, when the blossom is gone and the flower is ripening, the pruning knife does its work at exactly its moment, and the cut branches are left to the birds of summer and the beasts of winter. And the burden ends not with Cush destroyed but with Cush arriving, at that time “gifts will be brought to the LORD of Hosts”, carried by the tall feared nation itself to Mount Zion, the place of the Name. The burdens are only half done, and already two of them have ended at Zion's door: Philistia's envoys pointed to the refuge, Cush's envoys bringing the gifts themselves. Egypt is next, and her ending will be the most astonishing of all.

title: Egypt My People
subtitle: Isaiah 19
description: The LORD rides into Egypt, and the burden ends with Egypt called My people.
paragraphs: The Egypt burden opens with the last arrival Egypt's religion ever expected: “Behold, the LORD rides on a swift cloud; He is coming to Egypt. The idols of Egypt will tremble before Him, and the hearts of the Egyptians will melt within them.” What follows is a dismantling in layers, and the first layer is Egypt against itself: “I will incite Egyptian against Egyptian; brother will fight against brother”, neighbor against neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom, until the spirit of the Egyptians is emptied out and their counsel is frustrated into consulting the very idols that are trembling. The Nile itself is struck, and a dried Nile in Egypt is not a metaphor: “The waters of the Nile will dry up, and the riverbed will be parched and empty.” Canals stink, reeds wither, fishermen mourn over empty nets, flax workers and weavers of fine linen turn pale; the economy of the river dies with the river. And the famed wisdom of Egypt, the counsel Pharaohs boasted of from the eastern kings, is audited and found empty: “The princes of Zoan are mere fools; Pharaoh’s wise counselors give senseless advice.” “Where are your wise men now?” “The LORD has poured into her a spirit of confusion”, and Egypt staggers in everything she does like a drunkard in his own vomit, head and tail, palm and reed, nothing left that can act.

Then the burden performs the movement this whole section of the book keeps performing, and performs it further for Egypt than for any other nation. Five cities in the land of Egypt will speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of Hosts; one of them will be called the City of the Sun. There will be an altar to the LORD in the center of the land of Egypt and a pillar to Him at her border, a sign and a witness in the exodus land itself; and the exodus pattern is deliberately run in reverse inside it, Egypt now the oppressed who cry out: “When they cry out to the LORD because of their oppressors, He will send them a savior and defender to rescue them.” “The LORD will make Himself known to Egypt, and on that day Egypt will acknowledge the LORD.” They will worship with sacrifices and offerings, make vows and fulfill them. The striking comes with its purpose attached: “the LORD will strike Egypt with a plague; He will strike them but heal them. They will turn to the LORD, and He will hear their prayers and heal them.” Strike and heal in one sentence, the plagues of the exodus re-read as surgery.

And then the verse the whole burden section has been driving toward since Babylon, the highway: “In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria. The Assyrians will go to Egypt, and the Egyptians to Assyria. The Egyptians and Assyrians will worship together.” Egypt and Assyria, the two empires that take turns crushing Israel across the whole book, on one road, worshiping together, with Israel between them not as the battlefield but as the third partner: “In that day Israel will join a three-party alliance with Egypt and Assyria”, and the blessing God speaks over the arrangement assigns each nation one of Israel's own covenant titles, as though the titles were large enough to go around: “Blessed be Egypt My people, Assyria My handiwork, and Israel My inheritance.” My people, the name Lo-ammi's generation heard reversed, given to Egypt. My handiwork, the potter's title, given to Assyria. Israel keeps My inheritance, last in the list and first in nothing, and the burden ends with the three-way blessing standing in the text, unretracted, on the far side of every judgment the book has pronounced on all three nations.

Chapter twenty brings the horizon back to the present tense, and the sign it records is the most physically costly in the prophets. Two years before Assyria's commander takes Ashdod, God speaks through Isaiah: “Go, remove the sackcloth from your waist and the sandals from your feet.” And Isaiah does so, and keeps doing so, “walking around naked and barefoot” for three years, the prophet's own stripped body posted in Jerusalem as a living omen of what Assyrian captivity does to a people: “Just as My servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and omen against Egypt and Cush”, so the king of Assyria will lead Egypt's captives and Cush's exiles away, young and old, naked and barefoot, to Egypt's shame. The nations Judah is leaning on will be paraded past in the uniform of the defeated, and the coastal peoples who counted Egypt their insurance will read the omen and say the thing the whole burden section was written to make Judah say first: “See what has happened to our source of hope, those to whom we fled for help and deliverance from the king of Assyria! How then can we escape?” The burdens against the nations are finished when they come home. The next one is addressed to Jerusalem itself.

title: Watchman, What of the Night?
subtitle: Isaiah 21
description: From the watchtower: Babylon fallen, Dumah's unanswered night, Shebna displaced, and Tyre's seventy years.
paragraphs: The last three burdens are told from a watchtower, and the first of them gives the watchman his most famous post. A dire vision is declared against the Desert by the Sea, Babylon under her desert name, and the prophet's body registers it before his mind does, anguish like labor, a heart faltering, the twilight he loved turned to horror. Inside the vision the besieged city is at dinner: “They prepare a table, they lay out a carpet, they eat, they drink! Rise up, O princes, oil the shields!” The order to post the lookout comes, the riders are catalogued, teams of horsemen, donkeys, camels, and the lookout reports what a watchman reports, endurance first: “Day after day, my lord, I stand on the watchtower; night after night I stay at my post.” Then the horsemen come in pairs, and the answer goes up the tower: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon! All the images of her gods lie shattered on the ground!” Fallen, fallen, the doubling that the New Testament's last book will pick up about the same city, and here it is spoken first about a Babylon whose fall Isaiah's generation would not see, announced to a people the prophet addresses as crushed grain: O my people, crushed on the threshing floor, I tell you what I have heard from the LORD of Hosts.

Dumah's burden is eleven words of question and a watchman's refusal to answer it simply. From Seir, in Edom's hills, a voice calls across the dark: “Watchman, what is left of the night? Watchman, what is left of the night?” The doubled question gets the book's most honest timetable: “Morning has come, but also the night. If you would inquire, then inquire. Come back yet again.” Morning and night both, inquiry welcomed, closure refused; the watchman will still be at his post when the questioner returns, and the night is not required to be over for the morning to be real. Arabia's fugitives are told to be fed in the thickets by the dwellers of Tema, water for the thirsty and food for the refugees, while Kedar's glory is given one hired worker's year to expire. The burdens are turning south and east, smaller nations, shorter oracles, and then, without announcement, the watchtower looks down at its own city.

The burden against the Valley of Vision is against Jerusalem, and it opens on the rooftops, the whole city up on them in a mood the prophet cannot read as anything but revelry over a siege: your slain did not die by the sword or in battle, your rulers fled together and were captured without a bow, and Isaiah's response is the one Jonah never gave and Hosea gave for Israel, grief in the first person: “Turn away from me, let me weep bitterly! Do not try to console me over the destruction of the daughter of my people.” The indictment that follows is a precise piece of accounting from the Assyrian siege preparations: the weapons in the House of the Forest inspected, the breaches in David's walls counted, houses torn down to fortify the wall, the reservoir built between the walls for the ancient pool's water, every measure competent and every measure damned by the one omission: “but you did not look to the One who made it, or consider Him who planned it long ago”. On the day God called for weeping and sackcloth, the city answered with butchering and wine and the slogan the apostle Paul will later quote as the creed of despair: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!” And the verdict pronounced over the slogan is the harshest sentence in the burdens, spoken into the prophet's hearing: “Until your dying day, this sin of yours will never be atoned for”.

Shebna, the steward in charge of the palace, is then singled out of the crowd for a personal oracle, the only named courtier in the burdens: what is a palace steward doing carving himself a tomb in the heights, chiseling his resting place in the rock like a king? He will be seized, rolled into a ball, and slung into a wide land to die far from his tomb, a disgrace to his master's house, and his robe and sash and authority will be transferred to Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the servant on whose shoulder the book lays its most durable compliment: “I will place on his shoulder the key to the house of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open.” A father to Jerusalem, a peg driven into a firm place, a throne of glory, and then the oracle does the honest thing the court would not: the peg itself gets a expiry date: “the peg driven into a firm place will give way; it will be sheared off and fall”, and the load hung on it will be cut down. Even the best official in Isaiah's Jerusalem is a peg, not the foundation; the cornerstone is elsewhere in the book, and it is not a courtier.

Tyre closes the roll of nations, the merchant princess of the sea, her ships of Tarshish wailing for a harbor that no longer exists. Her question is asked in her own defense: “Who planned this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose traders are princes, whose merchants are renowned on the earth?” The answer humbles the sea as Babylon's fall humbled the land: “The LORD of Hosts planned it, to defile all its glorious beauty, to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.” Seventy years she will be forgotten, the span of a king's life, then restored to her trade like the forgotten harlot of the song taking up her harp to be remembered, and her ending is the burdens' ending, commerce itself converted: “Yet her profits and wages will be set apart to the LORD; they will not be stored or saved, for her profit will go to those who live before the LORD, for abundant food and fine clothing.” The nations' section closes with Tyre's money feeding God's people. The next movement widens past nations altogether, to the earth itself under judgment, and the feast that answers it.

title: The Feast on the Mountain
subtitle: Isaiah 24
description: The whole earth under judgment, and on the mountain a feast that swallows death.
paragraphs: Chapter twenty-four widens the lens past every border the burdens named, to the earth itself: “Behold, the LORD lays waste the earth and leaves it in ruins. He will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants”. The curse consumes without respect of ranks, the text insisting on the leveling in pairs, priest and people, master and servant, mistress and maid, buyer and seller, lender and borrower, creditor and debtor, all of it leveled under one sentence: “The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and fades; the exalted of the earth waste away.” The legal ground is stated as plainly as the ruin: “The earth is defiled by its people; they have transgressed the laws; they have overstepped the decrees and broken the everlasting covenant.” Vineyards languish, mirth's instruments fall silent, strong drink turns bitter to its drinker, and the unnamed city that stands for all of them gets the emptiest name in the book: “The city of chaos is shattered; every house is closed to entry.” Joy itself drains out of the world: the tambourine stops, the noise of the revelers stops, the harp stops, and what is left of the earth is a gleaning, an olive tree beaten to its last few berries at the very top.

But the gleanings sing. From the west, from the islands of the sea, voices rise over the desolation praising the majesty of the LORD and shouting the book's strangest doxology in a ruined world: “Glory to the Righteous One.” And Isaiah, alone of the choir, answers with the outburst the series has heard from him at every stage, grief refusing the program: “I am wasting away! I am wasting away! Woe is me.” The treacherous deal treacherously, terror and pit and snare wait for the inhabitants of the earth, the floodgates of heaven open, the foundations of the earth shake, the earth is utterly shattered and reels like a drunkard and sways like a shack, the transgression lying heavy on it until it falls and does not rise again. The punishment reaches above the earth that day, to the host of heaven itself, kings gathered like prisoners into a pit and punished after many days. And then the movement does what chapter two did, ending the devastation on a throne: “The moon will be confounded and the sun will be ashamed; for the LORD of Hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and before His elders with great glory.” The sun ashamed, because it is outshone.

Chapter twenty-five is the song that reign answers with, and it is personal in a way the ruins were not: “O LORD, You are my God! I will exalt You; I will praise Your name.” “For You have worked wonders”, the singer says, “plans formed long ago”, wonders that were plans, faithfulness that was exact. The ruthless breath is named as a storm and answered as a shelter: “For You have been a refuge for the poor, a stronghold for the needy in distress, a refuge from the storm, a shade from the heat.” The song's God is the poor's refuge, the same commission the vineyard song was given in chapter five, the widows and orphans of chapter one now sheltered under the song itself. And on the mountain where the glory reigns, the book sets the meal it has been traveling toward since the nations began to stream uphill in chapter two: “On this mountain the LORD of Hosts will prepare a lavish banquet for all the peoples, a feast of aged wine, of choice meat, of finely aged wine.” All the peoples, the burden list itself invited to dinner.

What the feast destroys is not a nation. It is the covering: “On this mountain He will swallow up the shroud that enfolds all peoples, the sheet that covers all nations”. And the covering's name is given in the book's most far-reaching sentence, the one the New Testament quotes verbatim at the end of its resurrection chapter, standing here at the feast's center: “He will swallow up death forever. The Lord GOD will wipe away the tears from every face and remove the disgrace of His people from the whole earth. For the LORD has spoken.” Death swallowed, tears wiped, disgrace removed, and the song gives the saved their own line to say over the meal, a line about waiting that vindicates every watchman in the book: “Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He has saved us. This is the LORD for whom we have waited. Let us rejoice and be glad in His salvation.” Isaiah's sealed-up waiting in chapter eight, the watchman's long night in chapter twenty-one, are answered at a table. The song ends on Moab, the proud neighbor of the weeping burden, her pride trodden like straw in a dung pile and her high walls ended where the book's proud always land: “The high-walled fortress will be brought down, cast to the ground, into the dust.” The mountain, meanwhile, is where its feasts are held. The next chapter opens inside a strong city, singing back.

title: Your Dead Will Live
subtitle: Isaiah 26
description: A song of the strong city, an honest prayer, Leviathan slain, and the great shofar gathering.
paragraphs: Chapter twenty-six opens with a song Judah will sing in that day, and its first image is a city whose defenses are not masonry: “We have a strong city; salvation is established as its walls and ramparts.” “Open the gates so a righteous nation may enter”, a nation defined by the quality Judah kept failing: remaining faithful. And the song states, in its most memorized sentence, the interior condition the whole book has been prescribing since the aqueduct: “You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You.” “Trust in the LORD forever, because GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal.” Rock eternal, the fixed thing under a city whose kings kept shaking like trees; Ahaz inspected a reservoir and would not trust, and the song's city trusts and is kept. The proud are brought down, the lofty city laid low to the dust where the feet of the oppressed walk over it, and the level path of the righteous is walked by a people whose confession names what they are actually waiting for: “Yes, we wait for You, O LORD; we walk in the path of Your judgments. Your name and renown are the desire of our souls.” “For when Your judgments come upon the earth, the people of the world learn righteousness.” Grace, the song admits, does not teach the wicked; show favor to the wicked and he does not learn righteousness, but judgment instructs the world. Even the increase of the nation is re-read as labor pains: they writhed and gave birth to wind, brought no salvation to the earth, and their dead did not rise, until the song reaches embodied resurrection: “O LORD, You will establish peace for us. For all that we have accomplished, You have done for us.”

The confession's depth is in its honesty about prayer under discipline: in their distress “they sought You”, and “they poured out a quiet prayer”, no volume left in them, like a woman in labor crying out, and the admission stands unedited that it produced wind. Which is why the promise that answers it is the chapter's glory and the movement's high point, God's voice breaking into the song with the book's plainest resurrection sentence: “Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust! For your dew is like the dew of the morning, and the earth will bring forth her dead.” Dust, the address of every corpse in the book, is told to sing. The dew of the morning does what dew does to dry ground, and the earth itself becomes a womb giving back her dead. Then the tone turns pastoral and urgent in the same breath, an instruction for the interval between the promise and its morning: “Go, my people, enter your rooms and shut your doors behind you. Hide yourselves a little while until the wrath has passed.” A little while, hiding rooms, the wrath with an expiry, and on the far side of it the LORD coming out of His place to punish the earth and expose her bloodshed, the slain no longer covered by the ground that drank them.

Chapter twenty-seven opens on the chaos monster the movement's first chapter darkened the sky with: Leviathan the serpent, the dragon of the sea, met at last by the sword described in three adjectives: “the LORD will take His sharp, great, and mighty sword”. Judgment on Leviathan is the verse, and then, without transition, the book sings the vineyard again, and everything about the song has changed since chapter five. “Sing about a fruitful vineyard”, the invitation is now; the sour grapes are gone, and the Gardener sings His own husbandry in the first person: “I, the LORD, am its keeper; I water it continually. I guard it night and day so no one can disturb it”. The hedge torn down in chapter five has become a Keeper standing in it around the clock. His anger has a budget now: He wishes the briers and thorns of the old song were set before Him in battle so He could burn them together; or let them take refuge in Him and make peace, the two options stated like terms of surrender, peace offered to the thorns themselves. And Jacob, who in chapter five brought forth sour fruit for all his tending, is promised the opposite harvest in the opposite direction: “In the days to come, Jacob will take root. Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit.” The vineyard's fruit fills the world. The altar stones of Israel's idolatry are pulverized like chalk in the same chapter, no Asherah poles left standing, and God's controversy with His own people is given its limit in the same breath: “By warfare and exile You contended with her”, measured warfare, a controversy with a scale in its hand, neither the measure of Egypt nor of the nations that oppressed her.

The movement ends on the shofar. Israel scattered from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt will be gathered the way grain is gleaned, one by one, and the instrument of their gathering is a blast: “And in that day a great ram’s horn will sound, and those who were perishing in Assyria will come forth with those who were exiles in Egypt. And they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.” Perishing in Assyria, exiled in Egypt, the two empires of the three-way blessing, their captives coming home to worship on the mountain where the feast is spread. The book's little apocalypse is over; its songs have outlasted its devastation, as the outline promised. What follows is a return to the immediate horizon, to drunk priests and a drunken policy, and the strangest schoolroom in the prophets.

title: The Cornerstone in Zion
subtitle: Isaiah 28
description: A drunken garland, vomit-covered tables, a covenant with death, and a cornerstone measured true.
paragraphs: The last movement of Isaiah's first half opens with a garland, and the garland is drunk: “Woe to the majestic crown of Ephraim’s drunkards, to the fading flower of his glorious splendor”, a fading flower worn by men overcome by wine, set on the head of the fertile valley. The crown has an appointment with a foot. “Behold, the Lord has one who is strong and mighty. Like a hailstorm or destructive tempest, like a driving rain or flooding downpour, he will smash that crown to the ground.” The fading flower will be eaten like the season's first ripe fig: “Whoever sees it will take it in his hand and swallow it.” Assyria eats Samaria in a gulp. And against the eaten crown the chapter sets the replacement, the book's remnant theology worn as jewelry: “On that day the LORD of Hosts will be a crown of glory, a diadem of splendor to the remnant of His people”, and more than jewelry, “a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and a strength to those who repel the onslaught at the gate”. God's people stop wearing flowers and start wearing Him.

Then the woe comes home to Jerusalem's own clergy, and it is the movement's most disgusting paragraph, stated flatly: “Priests and prophets reel from strong drink and are befuddled by wine.” They stumble in vision and in judgment, errand-runners of God too drunk to run straight: “For all their tables are covered with vomit; there is not a place without filth.” The prophet's sermon is then reviewed by its audience, and the review is preserved, because it becomes the judgment itself. They mock the teaching as baby food: “Whom is He trying to teach? To whom is He explaining His message? To infants just weaned from milk?” Their parody of his preaching style is quoted verbatim, precepts chanted like a nursery rhyme: “Order on order, order on order, line on line, line on line; a little here, a little there.” God's answer accepts the description and turns it into the sentence: since the plain word was refused, the word will come in a foreigner's accent, through Assyrian, and the message they chanted back as gibberish will become gibberish to them in fact, so that they go and fall backward, injured, ensnared, captured. What the mockery missed is stated inside the refused lines themselves: “This is the place of rest, let the weary rest; this is the place of repose.” But they would not listen.

Against the scoffers who rule Jerusalem, the chapter names their actual theology, a foreign policy dressed as a death pact: “We have made a covenant with death; we have fashioned an agreement with Sheol.” Egypt diplomacy, in their own words, insurance against the overwhelming scourge, “because we have made lies our refuge and falsehood our hiding place”. And into the middle of their actuarial religion God speaks the most architectural sentence in the book: “See, I lay a stone in Zion, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation; the one who believes will never be shaken.” A cornerstone laid against a covenant, belief against insurance, placed in Zion while the scoffers are still negotiating with Sheol. His construction instruments are not theirs: “I will make justice the measuring line and righteousness the level. Hail will sweep away your refuge of lies, and water will flood your hiding place.” “Your covenant with death will be dissolved, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand.” The scourge will pass through morning after morning, understanding will arrive as sheer terror, and their insurance policy gets a proverb for a payout: “Indeed, the bed is too short to stretch out on, and the blanket too small to wrap around you.” At Mount Perazim and Gibeon, where God once fought for Israel against her enemies, He now rises to fight against her, and the book names the oddity honestly: “to do His work, His strange work, and to perform His task, His disturbing task”.

The chapter ends in a farmyard, in the book's most patient piece of teaching. A farmer does not plow forever; he levels and sows, caraway and cumin and wheat and barley each in its place, his God instructing him. Caraway is not threshed with a sledge or cumin crushed under a cartwheel; the stick and the rod are fitted to the grain, bread grain is ground but not endlessly threshed, and the wheels pass over without crushing. Judgment, the parable says, is calibrated agriculture, and its source gets the final line of the chapter: “This also comes from the LORD of Hosts, who is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.” Chapter twenty-nine then besieges Ariel, David's altar city, reduced by her own God to something like an altar hearth, her voice whispering from the dust like a ghost's, before the besiegers themselves vanish like a hungry man's dream of eating: “as when a hungry man dreams he is eating, then awakens still hungry; as when a thirsty man dreams he is drinking, then awakens faint and parched.” And the sealed scroll goes from hand to hand, the literate pleading the seal, the illiterate pleading illiteracy, while the diagnosis of the whole blindness is spoken over the worship: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me. Their worship of Me is but rules taught by men.” “Therefore I will again confound these people with wonder upon wonder. The wisdom of the wise will vanish, and the intelligence of the intelligent will be hidden.” The potters who assure themselves God cannot see will be answered by a transformed world where Lebanon becomes an orchard and the scroll becomes readable at last: “On that day the deaf will hear the words of the scroll, and out of the deep darkness the eyes of the blind will see.” “The humble will increase their joy in the LORD, and the poor among men will rejoice in the Holy One of Israel.” And the movement's scoffers get the last word over themselves: “Then the wayward in spirit will come to understanding, and those who grumble will accept instruction.”

title: By Repentance and Rest
subtitle: Isaiah 30
description: Salvation by repentance and rest, refused for horses; Assyria burns at the breath of God.
paragraphs: The fifth woe of the movement is addressed to children, and the charge is not rebellion by sword but by itinerary: “Woe to the rebellious children”, “to those who carry out a plan that is not Mine, who form an alliance, but against My will”. The plan is diplomacy. “They set out to go down to Egypt without asking My advice, to seek shelter under Pharaoh’s protection and take refuge in Egypt’s shade.” Without asking My advice: the consultations at the aqueduct in chapter seven have become an embassy in chapter thirty, princes at Zoan, envoys arrived in Hanes, and the return on the investment is announced before the gifts are unpacked: “But Pharaoh’s protection will become your shame, and the refuge of Egypt’s shade your disgrace.” The burden against the beasts of the Negev follows the caravan on its route, donkeys and camels loaded with wealth moving through lion country and viper country, through hardship and distress, to purchase the help of a people of no profit. Egypt is given her nickname in passing, and it is a demotion worthy of the whole policy: “Egypt’s help is futile and empty; therefore I have called her Rahab Who Sits Still.” Rahab, the great sea monster of Egypt's boasting, reclassified by God as the dragon who does nothing.

The message is then ordered into the archive, because its audience has already voted against hearing it: “Go now, write it on a tablet in their presence and inscribe it on a scroll; it will be for the days to come, a witness forever and ever.” The people to be witnessed against are described by their own editorial policy, and the book preserves their instructions to the press: “Stop seeing visions!” “Do not prophesy to us the truth! Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions.” And the demand underneath the demand, the one the whole section exists to expose: “Get out of the way; turn off the road. Rid us of the Holy One of Israel!” Rid us of the Holy One of Israel. The signature title is named as the obstacle; the people who call God theirs want Him out of the road. Their iniquity is then imaged as structural failure, a wall already going: “this iniquity of yours is like a breach about to fail, a bulge in a high wall, whose collapse will come suddenly”, in an instant, and the breaking is a potter's jar: “It will break in pieces like a potter’s jar, shattered so that no fragment can be found.” Not a shard left big enough to scoop coals or skim water. The rejection is aimed at one specific message, and chapter fifteen of this episode quotes it whole, because it is the sentence the whole movement turns on: “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence”. “but you were not willing.”

Their counteroffer is cavalry: they will flee on horses, they say, and the answer repossesses their own sentence, therefore you will flee, and your pursuers will be faster, until a thousand flee at the threat of one and the nation is left like a flagpole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill, a signpost with no army under it. And then the chapter does the thing no one in it has asked for, in the verse that follows the refusal without a pause for breath: “Therefore the LORD longs to be gracious to you; therefore He rises to show you compassion, for the LORD is a just God. Blessed are all who wait for Him.” Longs to be gracious, addressed to the people who just demanded to be rid of Him; the waiting they refused is pronounced a blessing over their refusal.
