The promises pile up past the policy's failure: weeping ended, prayer answered at the sound of the cry, the bread of adversity and the water of affliction given with a Teacher who will hide no longer, “your Teacher will no longer hide Himself”, and a voice behind the walker at every crossroads: “This is the way. Walk in it.” The silver-plated idols of the alliance season will be defiled by their own owners' hands: “You will throw them away like menstrual cloths”, telling them to be gone, and rain returns to the sown ground, cattle graze wide, streams run on every high hill in the day of great slaughter, and the light is multiplied sevenfold “on the day that the LORD binds up the brokenness of His people and heals the wounds He has inflicted”. The wounds He has inflicted, bound up by the same hands: the book does not pretend the surgery was someone else's.

The chapter closes on the other patient. The Name of the LORD comes from afar in burning anger, His breath a rushing torrent up to the neck, sifting the nations in a sieve of destruction, and Assyria, the terror the Egypt policy was invented to escape, is disposed of not by Judah's cavalry but at God's own voice: Assyria will be shattered at the voice of the LORD, struck with His scepter, and every stroke lands to festival music, tambourines and lyres, as though the battle were a feast the people are only watching. And underneath the festival stands the fire built for the empire's master, Topheth, the burning place outside Jerusalem's wall, repurposed in advance for the king of Assyria: “For Topheth has long been prepared; it has been made ready for the king.” Deep and wide, fire and wood in plenty, and the match is God's own breath: “The breath of the LORD, like a torrent of burning sulfur, sets it ablaze.” Egypt sits still, Assyria burns on schedule, and the rebellious children are offered, in the same chapter, a Teacher who will not hide and a road with a voice on it. The next episode takes up the alliance one last time, and lets the king in his beauty be seen instead.

title: The King in His Beauty
subtitle: Isaiah 31
description: The last woes fall on Egypt-trusters and the destroyer, and eyes behold the King in His beauty.
paragraphs: The policy gets its third woe, and the charge is reduced to a gaze: “Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who rely on horses, who trust in their abundance of chariots and in their multitude of horsemen. They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD.” Horses are the issue only because eyes are. The alliance's theological error is then stated as a taxonomy, the cleanest sentence in the whole Egypt debate: “But the Egyptians are men, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit. When the LORD stretches out His hand, the helper will stumble, and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together.” Men, not God; flesh, not spirit; helper and helped falling in one heap when the hand comes out. Against that arithmetic God posts two pictures of Himself, and neither of them is negotiable. A lion over its prey, unimpressed by the posse: “Like a lion roaring or a young lion over its prey”, He is not terrified by the shepherds' shouting or subdued by their clamor; “so the LORD of Hosts will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights”. And a mother bird: “Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem. He will shield it and deliver it; He will pass over it and preserve it.” Pass over, the exodus word, spoken over the city Isaiah's generation is endangering: the destroyer of Egypt's firstborn becomes the covering of Jerusalem. The invitation inside the threat is one line long, return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled, and the day of idolatry's owners will throw away their own silver and gold with their own hands.

Assyria's end is given its mechanism in advance, and the mechanism is an absence: “Then Assyria will fall, but not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals.” Not by the sword of man. The empire that gathered nations like eggs will be undone by no human army, its rock passing away for fear, its princes panicking at a battle standard, and the oracle signs itself with the address of the fire: the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, whose furnace is in Jerusalem. Chapter thirty-two answers the fallen crown of chapter twenty-eight with the portrait the whole book has been missing: “Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule with justice.” “Each will be like a shelter from the wind, a refuge from the storm, like streams of water in a dry land, like the shadow of a great rock in an arid land.” Leadership as weather protection, the exact opposite of the storm kings: eyes unstopped, ears listening, the rash mind understanding, the stammering tongue fluent; the fool no longer called noble, the scoundrel no longer respected, a society whose titles have been recalibrated by truth, because a noble man makes honorable plans and stands up for worthy causes. The complacent women of the city are summoned to tremble a year out from a failed harvest, the palace forsaken, the watchtower a cave for wild donkeys, and the whole desolation is given a hinge word: “until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high. Then the desert will be an orchard, and the orchard will seem like a forest.” Until. The wilderness becomes justice's address, the fertile field righteousness's home, “The work of righteousness will be peace; the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever.” Quiet confidence, chapter thirty's refused prescription for salvation, is here installed as the permanent condition of the land.

Chapter thirty-three opens with the last woe of the section laid on the destroyer himself: “Woe to you, O destroyer never destroyed, O traitor never betrayed! When you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed. When you have finished betraying, you will be betrayed.” And the people's prayer inside the woe is the waiting doctrine learned at last: “O LORD, be gracious to us! We wait for You. Be our strength every morning and our salvation in time of trouble.” The envoys of peace weep bitterly in the streets, the treaty is broken, the land mourns, Lebanon is ashamed, and into the national collapse God speaks three words of timetable, now, now, now: now I will arise, now I will lift Myself up, now I will be exalted. The sinners in Zion are the ones who tremble at the arising, asking the question the cornerstone episode left hanging: “Who of us can dwell with a consuming fire? Who of us can dwell with everlasting flames?” The answer describes the resident rather than excusing him, the man who walks righteously and refuses bribes and stops his ears against murder plots; he will dwell on the heights, his food provided and his water assured. And then the chapter gives the movement its title, in the promise that gathers every theme on the road here: “Your eyes will see the King in His beauty and behold a land that stretches afar.” Your mind will ponder the former terror as an audit with no officials left to audit, the tally-clerk and the weigher and the tower-counter all gone, the insolent foreign speech heard no more.

Zion, in the closing vision, becomes the anti-Egypt and the anti-Assyria at once: Jerusalem a peaceful pasture, a tent that does not wander, pegs never pulled, cords never broken; the Majestic One there a place of rivers and wide canals wider than the Nile and safer, with no war galley rowing on them; and the constitution of the place stated in three offices held by one King: “For the LORD is our Judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our King. It is He who will save us.” The ropes of the old order hang slack and useless, the spoils of the broken empire are divided until even the lame carry plunder, and the final word over the city is a clean bill from the physician of chapter thirty: “The people who dwell there will be forgiven of iniquity.” The movement that opened with a drunk crown ends with a beautiful King and a forgiven city. What remains before the hinge chapters is one short, terrible pair: a sword with the whole earth on it, and a highway flowering through a desert.

title: The Way of Holiness
subtitle: Isaiah 34
description: Edom's uncreation answers to a blooming desert and the highway of holiness.
paragraphs: The last movement before the hinge opens with a summons wider than any courtroom yet: “Come near, O nations, to listen; pay attention, O peoples. Let the earth hear, and all that fills it, the world and all that springs from it.” The defendants are all nations, and the charge is not itemized, because the sentence is the story: “The LORD is angry with all the nations and furious with all their armies. He will devote them to destruction; He will give them over to slaughter.” The slain lie unburied, the mountains flow with blood, and the sky itself is dismantled: “All the stars of heaven will be dissolved. The skies will be rolled up like a scroll, and all their stars will fall like withered leaves from the vine, like foliage from the fig tree.” Then the cosmic sentence narrows to a single small nation, the way the whole book keeps narrowing: Edom, Jacob's brother nation, chosen as the exhibit of the universal wrath. The sword of the LORD, drunk in the heavens, comes down on Edom, and the battle is described in the language of the altar, deliberately: “The sword of the LORD is bathed in blood.” “For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom.” Lambs and goats, rams' kidneys, blood and fat, a slaughter liturgized into a sacrifice, and its calendar is the verse that gives the horror its purpose: “For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.”

Edom's land then undergoes the reverse of creation, in detail and at length, because this book does not do its hard places quickly. Streams turned to tar, soil to sulfur, a blazing pitch: “It will not be quenched”, “Its smoke will ascend forever”, and “no one will ever again pass through it”. Over the emptiness God stretches the surveyor's instruments of the cornerstone chapter, inverted: “The LORD will stretch out over Edom a measuring line of chaos and a plumb line of destruction.” Justice the measuring line in Zion; chaos the measuring line in Edom. Towers to thorns, fortresses to briers, jackals and ostriches and night creatures in the halls, owls gathering their broods under the shadow of a ruined kingdom, and the oracle underlines its own permanence with the strangest verification command in the prophets: “Search and read the scroll of the LORD: Not one of these will go missing, not one will lack her mate, because He has ordered it by His mouth, and He will gather them by His Spirit.” Check the scroll, the text says of itself; every creature on the desolation list will report for duty, because He has allotted their portion and His hand has measured it out. The desolation is as carefully administered as the salvation.

Chapter thirty-five is ten verses long, and it answers chapter thirty-four the way dawn answers night, image for image: “The wilderness and the dry land will be glad; the desert will rejoice and blossom like a rose.” Lebanon's glory, the tree library Ammon's kings boasted in, is given to the desert; Carmel and Sharon are moved into the wasteland; “They will see the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God.” The human orders that follow are pastoral triage for a frightened people, addressed to the helpers first: “Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!” And the sentence the strong are to carry to the trembling is prescribed verbatim: “Be strong, do not fear! Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.” The vengeance of chapter thirty-four and the salvation of chapter thirty-five are the same coming, viewed from two sides of the road. What the coming does to bodies is the chapter's central panel, the sealed scroll of chapter twenty-nine finally read aloud by the world itself: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped.” “Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy. For waters will gush forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.” Blind, deaf, lame, mute, the exact disabilities of Judah's idols and of Judah, healed in a landscape healed with them, parched ground turned pool, jackal-haunted ground turned grass and reeds and papyrus.

And through that landscape runs the road the whole book has been grading since chapter eleven: “And there will be a highway called the Way of Holiness.” Its traffic laws are the book's ethics in one verse: “The unclean will not travel it”, and “fools will not stray onto it”. Its safety is pastoral: “No lion will be there, and no vicious beast will go up on it. Such will not be found there, but the redeemed will walk upon it.” And its destination turns the movement's key from desolation all the way to procession: “So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.” Sorrow and sighing flee, the only fugitives in the chapter, outrun by joy on a road with no lions. The first half of the book ends there, on the threshold of the prose hinge, where the oracles step down into narrated history and an actual Assyrian army is at the actual wall, putting the whole book's counsel to its test: repentance and rest, or horses.

title: The Words on the Wall
subtitle: Isaiah 36
description: Sennacherib's spokesman preaches surrender at the aqueduct, and Hezekiah takes the letter into the temple.
paragraphs: The oracles step down into history at the exact spot where they began. In the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, Sennacherib of Assyria has taken every fortified city of Judah but one, and his field commander, the Rabshakeh, stops with a great army “by the aqueduct of the upper pool”, on the road to the Launderer's Field. It is the aqueduct of chapter seven, where Isaiah once met Hezekiah's father inspecting the same water for the same kind of siege and told him the two kings he dreaded were smoldering stubs. A generation later another king of Judah stands behind the same wall listening to another, larger empire explain why trust is folly, and this time the explanation is very good. The Rabshakeh's speech is quoted at length by the book because it deserves to be: it is the counter-sermon to everything Isaiah has preached, delivered in fluent Hebrew, over the wall, to the soldiers. His theology begins with Isaiah's own Egypt doctrine and improves the metaphor: “Look now, you are trusting in Egypt, that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it.” Egypt the sitting-still dragon has become a reed that wounds the hand that leans, and the Assyrian credits Hezekiah's reform as apostasy, offers two thousand horses Judah cannot rider, and claims, most cleverly of all, that the LORD Himself commissioned the invasion: Go up against this land and destroy it, the LORD said to me. The officials beg him to switch to Aramaic, the language of diplomacy, and he refuses and raises his voice, because the men on the wall, destined to eat their own dung and drink their own urine in the siege, are his real audience.

His terms are generous and his logic is a roll call: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he cannot deliver you.” “The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria”, he quotes Hezekiah's faith as the deception to be discarded. Make peace, come out, and “Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern”, “until I come and take you away to a land like your own”, deportation marketed as relocation, a land like your own with grain and wine. And the closer is the question the whole book has been building an answer to: “Who among all the gods of these lands has delivered his land from my hand? How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?” Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Samaria, the list is accurate. The people on the wall answer with the only obedience in the chapter, silence, because Hezekiah had commanded it, and the delegation goes in with torn clothes. Hezekiah tears his too, and puts on sackcloth, and goes into the house of the LORD, and sends to Isaiah. The king's message confesses the impasse in a labor image: “Today is a day of distress, rebuke, and disgrace; for children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them.” And the business of the message is prayer requested for a fraction: “Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that still survives.”

Isaiah's answer comes back at once, and it is the aqueduct sermon vindicated: “Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed Me.” “Behold, I will put a spirit in him so that he will hear a rumor and return to his own land, where I will cause him to fall by the sword.” The rumor arrives on schedule, Tirhakah of Cush marching out, and Sennacherib, called away, sends the argument in writing instead, the letter: your God is deceiving you, the list again, the gods of Gozan and Haran and Eden in Telassar, the kings of Hamath and Arpad. And Hezekiah performs the book's answer to written blasphemy with his hands: he receives the letter, reads it, goes up to the house of the LORD, and spreads it out before the LORD. What he prays over the open letter is the theological high point of the first half of the book, and it concedes the enemy's facts before it refutes his conclusion: “O LORD of Hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made the heavens and the earth.” “Incline Your ear, O LORD, and hear; open Your eyes, O LORD, and see.” Truly, the prayer admits, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all these countries; truly they burned the nations' gods, “for they were not gods, but only wood and stone”, the work of human hands. The Rabshakeh's roll call is answered god by god: they were burnable because they were made; the God of Israel is unburnable because He made. “And now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, O LORD, are God.”

The answering oracle dignifies the Assyrian with an arraignment. Because you have prayed, Isaiah sends, this is the word: “The Virgin Daughter of Zion despises you and mocks you; the Daughter of Jerusalem shakes her head behind you.” “Whom have you taunted and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel!” His own conquest speech is read back to him, the chariots on Lebanon's heights, the wells dug, Egypt's streams dried by his soles, and then the authorship of his whole career is reassigned in two lines: “Have you not heard? Long ago I ordained it; in days of old I planned it.” The axe of chapter ten is answered in prose, with the animal handling added: “I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth; I will send you back the way you came.” The sign to Hezekiah runs on harvest time, eat what grows of itself this year and next, sow and reap in the third, and the remnant doctrine flowers out of the siege ground in the direction it always pointed: “And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again take root below and bear fruit above.” “The zeal of the LORD of Hosts will accomplish this.” The siege verdict is total and oddly specific: “He will not enter this city or shoot an arrow into it.” Not an arrow. “I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David.” Then the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians, and the people got up the next morning to all the dead bodies. Sennacherib broke camp, went home to Nineveh, and in the temple of his god Nisroch his own sons put him to the sword, exactly where the rumor-oracle had filed him: fallen by the sword, in his own land, at worship. The field commander asked how the LORD could deliver Jerusalem. The chapter is the answer, in full, and it took one night.

title: Fifteen Years
subtitle: Isaiah 38
description: Fifteen years added, a king's own writing, and Babylonian envoys shown everything.
paragraphs: In those days, before the siege in the telling's order, the war comes inside the king's own body: Hezekiah is mortally ill, and Isaiah brings him the shortest oracle of his career: “Put your house in order, for you are about to die; you will not recover.” The man who spread an enemy's letter before God now has no document to spread; he turns his face to the wall and prays the prayer of a man presenting his record: “Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before You faithfully and with wholehearted devotion; I have done what is good in Your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly. Isaiah has not left the courtyard before the word comes back and turns him around: “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.” Fifteen years, numbered like a sentence reversed into a lease, and the defense of the city folded into the king's extension: I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria. The sign is the cosmos run backward on the palace architecture, the sun's shadow retreating up the stairway of Ahaz, the steps of the father who would not ask for a sign, climbed backward for the son who prayed for one: “I will make the sun’s shadow that falls on the stairway of Ahaz go back ten steps.” A lump of pressed figs on the boil is the medicine, and the king's question is the psalmist's question, what sign that I will go up to the house of the LORD again.

Then the chapter does something no other chapter in the first half of the book does: it hands the pen to the king. What follows is labeled a writing by Hezekiah after his illness and recovery, and Isaiah's book preserves it whole, a psalm inside the prophecy, the only royal composition in the volume. It begins at the wall he turned to: “In the prime of my life I must go through the gates of Sheol and be deprived of the remainder of my years.” “I will never again see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living; I will no longer look on mankind with those who dwell in this world.” His images are a working man's: a tent struck, a weaving cut: “My dwelling has been picked up and removed from me like a shepherd’s tent. I have rolled up my life like a weaver; He cuts me off from the loom; from day until night You make an end of me.” He composes himself till morning and a lion breaks his bones; he makes animal sounds for prayers: “I chirp like a swallow or crane; I moan like a dove. My eyes grow weak as I look upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my security.” Be my security: the king who banked a kingdom's defense on God's pledge asks for a personal guarantor, and the poem's theology arrives at the other side of the pit with the answer already in it: “O Lord, by such things men live, and in all of them my spirit finds life. You have restored me to health and have let me live.” “Surely for my own welfare I had such great anguish; but Your love has delivered me from the pit of oblivion, for You have cast all my sins behind Your back.” Behind Your back: the forgiven king locates his sins the way God once located Israel's, where they cannot be looked at. And his reason for wanting to live is a worship argument, stated as a fact about Sheol: “For Sheol cannot thank You; Death cannot praise You. Those who descend to the Pit cannot hope for Your faithfulness.” “The living, only the living, can thank You, as I do today; fathers will tell their children about Your faithfulness.” The poem ends at the instrument rack: “The LORD will save me; we will play songs on stringed instruments all the days of our lives in the house of the LORD.” All the days of our lives now means fifteen years, and the book lets the number hang over the song without comment.

What Hezekiah does with the fifteen years brings the ambassadors. Merodach-baladan of Babylon sends letters and a gift for the convalescent, a courtesy call from the rising power in the east, and Hezekiah, delivered king, shows the envoy everything: the silver and the gold, the spices and the precious oil, the entire armory, “There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them.” Isaiah's interview afterward is a model of the prophetic audit, three questions, no accusations: Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you? “They came to me from a distant land”, Hezekiah replies, “from Babylon.” What have they seen in your palace? “There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.” Then the word of the LORD of Hosts, the sentence that stands the book's second horizon up in a single oracle: “The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD.” “And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” Babylon: in Isaiah's day a courtesy caller; in the oracle, the coming treasury's address and the royal line's destination. The king who was given fifteen years answers the sentence on his own grandchildren with the most debated sentence of his reign, and the text gives his reasoning verbatim, leaving the judgment of it to the reader: “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” “At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.” Gratitude, resignation, or relief that the bill lands a generation down: the book does not say. It only records that the first half of Isaiah ends with exile announced and a king content not to live in it. The next words in the book, after a generation's silence, are the words the second horizon exists to deliver: Comfort, comfort My people.

title: Comfort, Comfort My People
subtitle: Isaiah 40
description: Comfort for the exile: a voice in the wilderness, a God beyond measure, strength for those who wait.
paragraphs: Between chapter thirty-nine and chapter forty, roughly a century and a half of story passes unspoken: the exile the ambassadors' visit promised has come and gone the long way, Jerusalem has fallen and lain ruined, and the people Isaiah addressed in the streets are being addressed now in Babylon, in the second horizon the outline named at this seam. The book does not explain the transition. It simply opens its mouth on the far side of the judgment and the first word is doubled, an imperative addressed to the comforters themselves: “Comfort, comfort My people”. My people, the name Lo-ammi's great-grandchildren hear restored in the mouth of the God their fathers were told to be rid of. The message for the ruined city is gentleness with an accounting attached: “Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her that her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned.” “For she has received from the hand of the LORD double for all her sins.” Double, the exile's arithmetic as the text itself states it, and then, immediately, a voice in a wilderness: “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert.” The highway system of the first half reaches its construction phase: “Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill made low; the uneven ground will become smooth, and the rugged land a plain.” “And the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it.” The road is not for Israel's escape. It is for God's arrival, and the whole species is on the roadside.

A second voice commissions the herald, and the exchange is preserved: Cry out. What should I cry out? And the answer sets the permanence ratio the whole second half runs on: “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field.” The grass withers, the flowers fall when the breath of the LORD blows on them; “The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.” Empires are grass; the sentence outlives the sentencing. Then the herald is posted, and the herald is the city itself: “Go up on a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news. Raise your voice loudly, O Jerusalem, herald of good news.” Lift it up, do not be afraid: “Here is your God!” The God who arrives down the graded highway comes with might and with His reward, and is described in the same breath as the warrior and as the shepherd: “He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart. He gently leads the nursing ewes.” Lambs in the arms, ewes led gently, the flock carried the way exiles are carried home: the arrival's strength is spent on transport.

Then the chapter builds its case, and the case is scale. The God who is coming is measured against everything the exiles can see: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, or marked off the heavens with the span of his hand?” Who has held the earth's dust in a basket, weighed mountains on a scale, hills with a balance; who was His counselor, who taught Him justice and knowledge and understanding. Babylon's gods are manufactured in the same chapter by craftsmen with gold overlays and silver chains, or by a poor man choosing rot-resistant wood and hiring a skilled craftsman to set up an idol that will not topple: manufactured gods with stability engineering, against a God who has never needed a teacher. “Surely the nations are like a drop in a bucket; they are considered a speck of dust on the scales”, Lebanon's forests insufficient for His firewood, her beasts for His offering: “All the nations are as nothing before Him; He regards them as nothingness and emptiness.” “He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth; its dwellers are like grasshoppers. He stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in.” Princes are blown on and wither like stubble, and the challenge is issued over the whole creation menagerie of Babylon: “To whom will you liken Me, or who is My equal?” “Lift up your eyes on high: Who created all these? He leads forth the starry host by number; He calls each one by name.” Not one of them is missing: the stars Babylon worshiped are a muster roll He calls by name.

The argument lands, at last, on the exiles' own complaint, which the text quotes back to them exactly as they have been saying it to each other: “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my claim is ignored by my God”. Hidden and ignored, the two charges of the deported. The rebuttal is not a theodicy lecture; it is a name and a promise: “The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He will not grow tired or weary; His understanding is beyond searching out.” “He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak.” Youths tire, young men stumble and fall, the empire's athletes exhaust; and the chapter ends with the prescription the first half kept issuing and the second half now guarantees, the waiting doctrine with wings on it: “But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint.” Run, and then walk: the promise descends from flight to a daily pace and holds at both ends, which is where exiles actually live. The chapter that follows opens a courtroom, and the God of the everlasting arms calls the nations' gods to testify.

title: Do Not Fear, O Jacob
subtitle: Isaiah 41
description: The courtroom of the nations: God speaks first to His servant, do not fear.
paragraphs: The courtroom of the second half assembles at the ends of the earth: “Be silent before Me, O islands, and let the peoples renew their strength. Let them come forward and testify; let us together draw near for judgment.” The case opens with a question about a conqueror, the man from the east whose career is the chapter's unnamed exhibit: “Who has aroused one from the east and called him to his feet in righteousness?” He hands nations over, subdues kings, turns armies to dust and chaff with sword and bow, pursues them in safety along paths his feet have barely touched, and the authorship question is asked over his whole campaign: “Who has performed this and carried it out, calling forth the generations from the beginning?” The answer assigns the conqueror the way chapter thirty-seven assigned Sennacherib: the LORD, “the first and the last”, I am He. The islands see the conqueror coming and tremble, and their response to fear is manufacturing: everyone helps his neighbor, encourages his brother to be strong, and the workshop chain is drawn with affection for its futility, the craftsman cheering the goldsmith, the hammer man cheering the anvil man, the weld pronounced good, and the finished god nailed down so it will not be toppled. The gods of the frightened are built by committees and stabilized with nails, and God's word turns from the workshop to the worm: “But you, O Israel, My servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, descendant of Abraham My friend”.

What is said to the chosen servant is the chapter's beating heart, and it is said with his full pedigree attached: brought from the ends of the earth, called from its farthest corners, “You are My servant”, “I have chosen and not rejected you”. And then the promise that gives this episode its title, the fear-oracle in its fullest form yet: “Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be afraid, for I am your God. I will strengthen you; I will surely help you; I will uphold you with My righteous right hand.” Immanuel's grammar again, God with us, now with a hand in the sentence: “For I am the LORD your God, who takes hold of your right hand and tells you: Do not fear, I will help you.” And the address refuses to flatter the recipient into dignity first: “Do not fear, O Jacob, you worm, O few men of Israel. I will help you”, declares the LORD. “Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel.” Worm Jacob, redeemed by the Holy One: the title the nation despised in chapter one is now the name of its Redeemer, and the worm is promised a promotion stranger than the shoot's: made into a threshing sledge new and sharp with many teeth, threshing mountains and reducing hills to chaff, rejoicing in the LORD while the wind carries his enemies off. The poor and needy of the book's long syllabus return in the same movement, tongues parched for water that is not there: “The poor and needy seek water, but there is none; their tongues are parched with thirst. I, the LORD, will answer them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them.” “I will open rivers on the barren heights, and fountains in the middle of the valleys. I will turn the desert into a pool of water, and the dry land into flowing springs.” Cedars and acacias, myrtles and olives, cypresses and elms and boxwood planted in the desert as evidence, “so that all may see and know, may consider and understand, that the hand of the LORD has done this and the Holy One of Israel has created it”.

Then the courtroom resumes, and the trial of the gods is conducted on the only evidence God accepts in this book: prediction. Present your case, says the LORD; submit your arguments, says the King of Jacob. Let the idols come and tell what will happen, or explain the former things so the court may know their outcome: “Tell us the things that are to come, so that we may know that you are gods.” “Yes, do something good or evil, that we may look on together in dismay.” Anything at all, the taunt runs, any act in either direction that would prove a pulse. The verdict is delivered before the defense rests: “Behold, you are nothing and your work is of no value. Anyone who chooses you is detestable.” And God's own evidence is entered in the conqueror again, raised from the north this time, from the rising of the sun, treading rulers like mortar and clay, with the courtroom question put to the silent benches: who declared this from the beginning, so that we may say he was right? No one announced it, no one foretold it, no one heard your words. I was the first to tell Zion, I gave Jerusalem a herald of good news, and when I look among the gods for a counselor there is no one, and when I ask them, they have nothing to say. The chapter closes with the bench empty and the verdict generalized past appeal: “See, they are all a delusion; their works amount to nothing; their images are as empty as the wind.” The servant who is chosen and not rejected will now be introduced by name and office, and the introduction begins with the quietest verb in the book: Behold.

title: Here Is My Servant
subtitle: Isaiah 42
description: Here is My Servant, who will not break a bruised reed; Israel, blind and plundered, is named servant too.
paragraphs: The second half's central figure is introduced the way the courtroom demanded, with evidence: “Here is My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One, in whom My soul delights. I will put My Spirit on Him, and He will bring justice to the nations.” The Spirit of the shoot of Jesse rests here again, and the office is the book's recurring one, justice to the nations, the thing chapter five's vineyard failed to grow and chapter thirty-two's king was promised to reign in. What distinguishes this bearer of the office is his volume: “He will not cry out or raise His voice, nor make His voice heard in the streets.” No shouting in the streets from the man the nations are waiting for, and his gentleness is specified by its two test cases, the already-damaged: “A bruised reed He will not break and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish; He will faithfully bring forth justice.” A bruised reed, fit only for breaking; a wick down to smoke, fit only for pinching out; the Servant's faithfulness is measured by what He declines to finish off. Nor will He need to be rescued from discouragement by His own prophecy: “He will not grow weak or discouraged before He has established justice on the earth. In His law the islands will put their hope.” The islands that trembled in the courtroom put their hope in His instruction, and the waiting world of the book gets its posture corrected toward a person.

The commission is then spoken to him directly, in the Creator's credentials: He who created the heavens and stretched them out, who gives breath to the people and life to those who walk in it, holds the Servant's hand the way He held Jacob's in chapter forty-one: “I, the LORD, have called you for a righteous purpose, and I will take hold of your hand. I will keep you and appoint you to be a covenant for the people and a light to the nations”. A covenant for the people, not a covenant keeper only: his person is the treaty. And the work is the book's disability list read as a job description: “to open the eyes of the blind, to bring prisoners out of the dungeon and those sitting in darkness out from the prison house”. Blind eyes opened, the sealed scroll of chapter twenty-nine made readable by a person; prisoners out, the captives of the burdens brought home by an office. The glory clause follows immediately, as if to fence the appointment: “I am the LORD; that is My name! I will not yield My glory to another or My praise to idols.” “Behold, the former things have happened, and now I declare new things. Before they spring forth I proclaim them to you.” New things, declared in advance: the prediction test of the courtroom, applied by God to His own announcement, and the response the chapter orders is a new song from the ends of the earth, islands and deserts and Kedar's villages and Sela's crags all raising the noise the Servant declines to make.

Then the tempo breaks, and God describes His own long restraint in the most startling self-portrait in the book: “I have kept silent from ages past; I have remained quiet and restrained. But now I will groan like a woman in labor; I will at once gasp and pant.” The silent God of the exile years, restraining Himself through the whole burning of His city, breaks the silence the way Hezekiah's children-at-the-birth image demanded, in labor: gasping, panting, laying waste mountains, turning rivers to dry land, draining marshes. And His first act in the noise is guidance, for the same blind of the Servant's job description: “I will lead the blind by a way they did not know; I will guide them on unfamiliar paths. I will turn darkness into light before them and rough places into level ground.” These things I will do, and I will not forsake them. The idols' clients, by contrast, molten images addressed as gods, will be turned back in utter shame, and the chapter pivots to the riddle it has been carrying since its first verse: “Listen, you deaf ones; look, you blind ones, that you may see!” “Who is blind but My servant, or deaf like the messenger I am sending? Who is blind like My covenant partner, or blind like the servant of the LORD?” Two servants now stand in the text, and the book does not merge them: the Servant who opens blind eyes, and the servant Israel, seeing many things and not keeping watch, ears open and not hearing, the LORD pleased for His righteousness' sake to magnify the law they would not obey.

The chapter's last paragraph gives the blind servant's condition its forensic summary: “But this is a people plundered and looted, all trapped in caves or imprisoned in dungeons.” Plunder with no one to rescue, loot with no one to say, Send them back. Who did this to Jacob is the question the exiles have asked Babylon for a generation, and the answer is the book's own: “Who gave Jacob up for spoil, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned?” Not Babylon's gods, not Babylon's strength: the LORD gave them up, because they were unwilling to walk in His ways and would not obey His law. “So He poured out on them His furious anger and the fierceness of battle. It enveloped them in flames, but they did not understand; it consumed them, but they did not take it to heart.” Did not understand, did not take it to heart: the burning lesson unlearned is the chapter's final diagnosis, spoken over the servant who cannot see straight at the exact point where the next chapter opens with the most tender address in the book, But now. The fire's students are about to be called by name.

title: You Are Mine
subtitle: Isaiah 43
description: You are Mine: witnesses called, former things forgotten, transgressions blotted out for God's own sake.
paragraphs: “But now, this is what the LORD says”, and the address that follows is the book's most personal sentence, spoken by the two titles that bracket Israel's whole existence, Creator and Former, He who created you, O Jacob, and He who formed you, O Israel: “Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by your name; you are Mine!” Called by name, the starry-host courtesy extended to the worm of chapter forty-one; and the redemption is immediately tested against the two elements of the first half, water and fire, the flood at the neck and the burning of the exile: “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you. When you walk through the fire, you will not be scorched; the flames will not set you ablaze.” The speaker identifies Himself by the title the nation despised and the fires could not burn: “For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior; I give Egypt for your ransom, Cush and Seba in your place.” Egypt, the reed, the shade, the sitting-still dragon, is now currency: given as ransom, Cush and Seba thrown in, and the exchange rate is justified in words no actuary would sign: “Because you are precious and honored in My sight, and because I love you, I will give men in exchange for you and nations in place of your life.” Precious and honored and loved, in God's sight, whatever the sight of the nations reported; and the ingathering is commanded to the compass points in the imperative, north ordered to give them up, south forbidden to hold them back: “Bring My sons from afar, and My daughters from the ends of the earth”, everyone called by My name and created for My glory.

The courtroom reconvenes, and Israel's role in it is formally assigned: the blind and deaf people are brought out as evidence, and the nations' witnesses are invited to vindicate their gods if they can. Against their silence stands the declaration: “You are My witnesses”, and My servant whom I have chosen, “so that you may consider and believe Me and understand that I am He”. Before Me no god was formed, and after Me none will come: “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me.” I alone decreed and saved and proclaimed, not some foreign god among you, and the irreversibility is stated like a law of the courtroom's physics: “Even from eternity I am He, and none can deliver out of My hand. When I act, who can reverse it?” Then the Redeemer applies the doctrine to Babylon by name, the courtesy callers of chapter thirty-nine coming back as fugitives: for your sake I will send to Babylon and bring them all as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice. The God who speaks it titles Himself for the occasion in one line: I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, and your King; and His résumé is the exodus itself, the God “who makes a way in the sea and a path through the surging waters”, who brought out Pharaoh's chariots and horses to lie down in the deep and never rise, extinguished, snuffed out like a wick.

And then this God, introduced by His greatest former thing, orders the former thing forgotten: “Do not call to mind the former things; pay no attention to the things of old.” “Behold, I am about to do something new; even now it is coming. Do you not see it? Indeed, I will make a way in the wilderness and streams in the desert.” The new thing outbids the exodus on its own ground, a way in the wilderness rather than the sea, water appearing where there was no water to divide; jackals and ostriches will honor Him for drink given in the desert, and the people formed for Himself will declare His praise. The chapter, however, is too honest to end on the promise, because the promise's recipients are introduced mid-reproach: “But you have not called on Me, O Jacob, because you have grown weary of Me, O Israel.” No sheep brought, no sacrifices honoring, no sweet cane bought with silver; God unburdened by their offerings and unwearied by their frankincense, and weariness itself reassigned to its rightful owner: “But you have burdened Me with your sins; you have wearied Me with your iniquities.” The worship ledger of chapter one inverted for good: the sacrifices were never the weight; the sins were.

And into that ledger God writes the verse the whole second half exists under: “I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more.” For My own sake: the blotting is not earned by the burdened or negotiated by the weary; it is located in God's own interest and name, and the offer to litigate remains open in the very next breath: Remind Me, let us argue the matter together; state your case, so that you may be vindicated. The audit of the case follows at once and it is not flattering: your first father sinned, and your spokesmen rebelled against Me, the sanctuary princes disgraced, Jacob devoted to destruction and Israel to reproach. That is the record on which the blotting stands. The chapter that began with You are Mine ends with the devotion to destruction still in the file and the blotting unretracted on top of it, which is, precisely, the book's definition of grace. The next chapter takes the forgiven people back to the workshop, to watch a god being made out of a log.

title: A Block of Wood
subtitle: Isaiah 44
description: The idol factory toured at length, and Cyrus named a shepherd before he is born.
paragraphs: The address softens before the argument sharpens: “But now listen, O Jacob My servant, Israel, whom I have chosen.” The Maker's voice, who formed you from the womb and who will help you: “Do not be afraid, O Jacob My servant, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen.” Jeshurun, the upright one, a pet name for Israel found in the song of Moses, revived here for the blind servant at his lowest. The promise attached to the name is liquid and spiritual in a single pour: “For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and currents on the dry ground. I will pour out My Spirit on your descendants, and My blessing on your offspring.” Willows by flowing streams, and the grandchildren introducing themselves by their allegiance: one will say, “I belong to the LORD”, another will take Jacob's name, and a third will write on his own hand that he is the LORD's, and take the name Israel for himself. Belonging, in the chapter's future, is something a man writes on his own hand. Then the King and Redeemer of Israel reintroduces Himself to the courtroom that has heard it all before: “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me.” The challenge stands, tell the future, and the witnesses are reminded of their commission: “Do not tremble or fear. Have I not told you and declared it long ago? You are My witnesses! Is there any God but Me? There is no other Rock; I know not one.”

Against that testimony the chapter sets the longest single scene in the book, and it is a factory tour. All makers of idols are nothing, their treasures worthless, their witnesses unable to see or comprehend, and the audit walks the floor. The blacksmith labors over the coals with his strong arms, forging his god between meals: “Yet he grows hungry and loses his strength; he fails to drink water and grows faint.” The god-maker faints at his work, which the text records without comment, because the comment is the fact. The woodworker measures and marks and shapes with chisel and compass, fashioning the likeness of man in all his glory to dwell in a shrine. Then the camera follows the raw material backward: the craftsman cuts down a cedar, or takes a cypress or an oak he let grow strong in the forest, or plants a laurel for the rain to raise. “It serves as fuel for man. He takes some of it to warm himself, and he kindles a fire and bakes his bread. He also fashions it into a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it.” Half the log warms him and roasts his meat, and he is satisfied, and says so: Ah, I am warm, I see the fire. “From the rest he makes a god, his graven image. He bows down to it and worships; he prays to it and says, “Save me, for you are my god.”” The rest. The leftover of the firewood, promoted to savior, asked to save by the man who carried it in from the woodpile.

The diagnosis is not cruelty; it is bewilderment at a closed system: they do not comprehend or discern, their eyes shut, their minds closed, and “no one considers in his heart, no one has the knowledge or insight to say” the sentence the whole satire has been setting up, the workshop prayer that would end the workshop: “I burned half of it in the fire, and I baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and I ate. Shall I make something detestable with the rest of it? Shall I bow down to a block of wood?” A block of wood: the chapter's title and the god's job description in the customer's own words, never spoken. “He feeds on ashes. His deluded heart has led him astray”, and he cannot deliver himself or bring himself to ask whether the thing in his right hand is a lie. That, says the book, is the whole tragedy of idolatry in one biography: not ignorance of God, but a question a man cannot afford to ask about his own dinner fire. And the pivot to Jacob is immediate, before the smoke clears: Remember these things, O Jacob, for you are My servant, O Israel: “I have made you, and you are My servant; O Israel, I will never forget you.” “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to Me, for I have redeemed you.” The heavens are ordered to sing about it, mountains and forests and every tree in them, because the LORD has redeemed Jacob and revealed His glory in Israel: the servant made by God is forgiven by God; the god made by the servant eats ashes with him.

The closing credential is a résumé read aloud: “I am the LORD, who has made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who by Myself spread out the earth”, who foils the signs of false prophets and makes fools of diviners and turns the wise men's knowledge into nonsense, and, the item that stakes everything, “who confirms the message of His servant and fulfills the counsel of His messengers”. His messengers' current counsel is then itemized in His own voice: of Jerusalem, “She will be inhabited”, and of the cities of Judah, “She will be rebuilt”, ruins restored, depths commanded dry. And the last item names the workman, a century and a half early and without hedging: of Cyrus, “My shepherd will fulfill all that I desire”, who says of Jerusalem, “She will be rebuilt”, and of the temple, “Let its foundation be laid”. Cyrus, the Persian not yet born when Isaiah's audience heard this, filed in the book as God's shepherd with a building permit for a temple still standing when the words were spoken. The next chapter is addressed to him by name.

title: Cyrus, His Anointed
subtitle: Isaiah 45
description: Cyrus, His anointed; clay warned before the potter; Babylon's gods carried away on animals.
paragraphs: “This is what the LORD says to Cyrus His anointed”, and the sentence contains its own scandal: anointed, messiah, a title the book has kept for Israel's kings and priests, laid on a Persian emperor who does not know the God anointing him. His right hand is grasped to subdue nations, disarm kings, and open doors that will not be shut, and the Almighty announces the itinerary like an advance man going ahead of the army: “I will go before you and level the mountains; I will break down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron.” “I will give you the treasures of darkness and the riches hidden in secret places, so that you may know that I am the LORD, the God of Israel, who calls you by name.” The conquests are tuition; the curriculum is knowing. And the reason Cyrus is chosen is stated to his face, lest he misread his own career: “For the sake of Jacob My servant and Israel My chosen one, I call you by name; I have given you a title of honor, though you have not known Me.” “I am the LORD, and there is no other; there is no God but Me. I will equip you for battle, though you have not known Me”, “so that all may know, from where the sun rises to where it sets, that there is none but Me”. The emperor is an instrument with an audience, sunrise to sunset, and the God wielding him owns both ends of the moral weather without apology: “I form the light and create the darkness; I bring prosperity and create calamity. I, the LORD, do all these things.”

The clay is then warned about complaining to the potter, in the movement's sharpest piece of household logic: “Woe to him who quarrels with his Maker”. “Does the clay ask the potter” what he is making; does the work announce that its maker has no hands; woe to the child who cross-examines his own begetting. Concerning things to come, do you question Me about My sons, or instruct Me in the work of My hands? The Maker's answer is His résumé, the earth made, man created, the heavens stretched by His hands, every host ordained, and then the policy re-stated without flinching: “I will raise up Cyrus in righteousness, and I will make all his ways straight. He will rebuild My city and set My exiles free, but not for payment or reward, says the LORD of Hosts.” Not for payment or reward: the only emancipator in the book who works unpaid, and Egypt's products and Cush's merchandise and the tall Sabeans will come over in chains confessing the courtroom's verdict through Israel's address: God is indeed with you, and there is no other God. “Truly You are a God who hides Himself, O God of Israel, the Savior.” The confession stands in the text unexplained, the hiddenness of God confessed by the book that reveals Him, and against the idol-makers departing in disgrace stands the permanence clause: “But Israel will be saved by the LORD with an everlasting salvation; you will not be put to shame or humiliated, to ages everlasting.” The Creator then testifies to His own candor: He did not create the earth to be empty but formed it to be inhabited; “I have not spoken in secret, from a place in a land of darkness.” “I, the LORD, speak the truth; I say what is right.” And the chapter signs with the oath and the invitation in consecutive breaths: “There is no other God but Me, a righteous God and Savior; there is none but Me.” “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.” “By Myself I have sworn; truth has gone out from My mouth, a word that will not be revoked: Every knee will bow before Me, every tongue will swear allegiance.”

Chapter forty-six opens on the day of Babylon's fall, and the picture is a refugee column of gods: “Bel crouches; Nebo cowers. Their idols weigh down beasts and cattle.” Babylon's great deities, Bel and Nebo, are luggage now, loaded on pack animals for evacuation, burdensome, a load to the weary animal, and the procession's end is the book's driest sentence on manufactured religion: the gods cower and crouch together, unable to relieve the burden, “but they themselves go into captivity”. The gods go into captivity. And over against the carried gods stands the carrying God, addressing the remnant by its carrying history: “Listen to Me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been sustained from the womb, carried along since birth.” “Even to your old age, I will be the same, and I will bear you up when you turn gray. I have made you, and I will carry you; I will sustain you and deliver you.” Made and carried, womb to gray hair: the entire doctrine is a contrast of transport. Their gods are lifted to a shoulder and carried along and set in place, “and there it stands, not budging from that spot. They cry out to it, but it does not answer; it saves no one from his troubles.” Israel's God lifts Israel to His own shoulder and carries them the whole journey, and answers.

The closing argument is the courtroom's last exhibit, memory itself: Remember this and be brave; take it to heart, you transgressors. “Remember what happened long ago, for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like Me.” “I declare the end from the beginning, and from ancient times what is still to come.” “My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish.” And the bird summoned to prove it is Cyrus again, without the name this time, the crest only: “I summon a bird of prey from the east, a man for My purpose from a far-off land. Truly I have spoken, and truly I will bring it to pass.” The stubborn are addressed last, far removed from righteousness, and the distance is closed in the chapter's final line, spoken to Zion as the whole movement's assurance: “I am bringing My righteousness near; it is not far away, and My salvation will not be delayed. I will grant salvation to Zion and adorn Israel with My splendor.” The bird of prey is coming from the east. What he will find when he arrives is Babylon herself, addressed next, on a throne she is ordered to vacate into the dust.

title: Leave Babylon
subtitle: Isaiah 47
description: Babylon's queen steps down to the dust, and Israel is told to leave her with singing.
paragraphs: The taunt song over Babylon is sung to a woman on a throne, and its first line is a change of furniture: “Go down and sit in the dust, O Virgin Daughter of Babylon. Sit on the ground without a throne, O Daughter of the Chaldeans! For you will no longer be called tender or delicate.” Millstones are put in the queen's hands, flour to grind, veil removed, skirt stripped, thigh bared to wade the streams, the labor of a slave girl assigned to the mistress of kingdoms with her shame exposed, and the vengeance announced without negotiation: I will take vengeance; I will spare no one. Into the middle of the dethronement the book inserts its doxology like a nameplate: Our Redeemer, “the LORD of Hosts is His name”, the Holy One of Israel, the Redeemer title spoken precisely where the redeemed are still under the queen's yoke. Sit in silence, she is told, and go into darkness, for you will no longer be called the queen of kingdoms. And God's charge against her is not that she conquered His people; it is how: “I was angry with My people; I profaned My heritage, and I placed them under your control. You showed them no mercy; even on the elderly you laid a most heavy yoke.” The rod of chapter ten is arraigned again, in a skirt this time: the instrument exceeded the assignment, mistook custody for ownership, and announced the mistake as policy: “I will be queen forever.” She did not take these things to heart or consider their outcome.

The queen's theology is quoted in her own words, because it is the exact sentence God has been claiming for Himself all book: “I am, and there is none besides me. I will never be a widow or know the loss of children.” I am, and none besides me: the Holy One's courtroom formula in the mouth of Babylon, which is the definition of the blasphemy this book prosecutes. Both disasters she has exempted herself from arrive together, in a moment, in a single day, loss of children and widowhood in full measure, in spite of the many sorceries and the potency of the spells. Her security doctrine is read back to her: you were secure in your wickedness; you said, No one sees me; your wisdom and knowledge led you astray, and the charm offensive she is counseled to attempt is the satire's last cruelty: stand with your spells, then, the ones you have wearied yourself with since youth; perhaps you will succeed; “You are wearied by your many counselors; let them come forward now and save you”, the astrologers, the monthly predictors, the star counters. “Surely they are like stubble; the fire will burn them up. They cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. There will be no coals to warm them or fire to sit beside.” No coals to warm them: the fire that ends Babylon's counselors will not even serve as a hearth, and her traders of a lifetime stray each in his own direction, and not one of them can save her. The queen of kingdoms sits in the dust with flour on her hands, and the sorcery department burns without giving off heat.

Chapter forty-eight turns from the queen to the congregation, and the address is an audit of names: house of Jacob, called by the name of Israel, descended from Judah, “who swear by the name of the LORD, who invoke the God of Israel”, and the audit's finding finishes the verse like a slap: “but not in truth or righteousness”. They lean on the God of Israel and call themselves after the holy city, and the God they lean on explains, once more and with unusual patience, why He has been predicting things in advance at all: because of the material the audience is made of. “For I knew that you are stubborn; your neck is iron and your forehead is bronze.” The predictions were published long ago so that when they came to pass Israel could not hand the credit to the molten god: “My idol has done this; my carved image and molten god has ordained it.” New things, hidden things, created now and not long ago, are announced for the same reason, so the rebel-from-birth people cannot say they knew them already. And the wrath that stubbornness has earned is deferred for a reason located in God, the same reason as the blotting of chapter forty-three: “For the sake of My name I will delay My wrath; for the sake of My praise I will restrain it, so that you will not be cut off.” “See, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction.” “For My own sake, My very own sake, I will act; for how can I let Myself be defamed? I will not yield My glory to another.” The furnace was a refinery, not an execution; the metal was tested, not consumed, and the refiner's motive is His own unstained name.

The chapter closes the movement with the ally and the exit. “Listen to Me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I have called: I am He; I am the first, and I am the last.” His hand founded the earth, His right hand spread the heavens, and when He summons them they stand up together, a muster the stars of Babylon never managed. Which of the idols foretold these things? None; but “The LORD’s chosen ally will carry out His desire against Babylon, and His arm will be against the Chaldeans.” I, even I, have spoken; I have called him; I have brought him; he will succeed in his mission. And then the Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, turns schoolmaster one last time before the door opens: “I am the LORD your God, who teaches you for your benefit, who directs you in the way you should go.” “If only you had paid attention to My commandments, your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like waves of the sea.” If only: the book's tenderest counterfactual, descendants like the sand and the grains of sand, a name never cut off. But the movement's last word is not the conditional; it is the command, shouted, with the new exodus already narrated as underway: “Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans!” Declare it with a shout of joy to the ends of the earth: “The LORD has redeemed His servant Jacob!” “They did not thirst when He led them through the deserts; He made water flow for them from the rock; He split the rock, and water gushed out.” Water from the rock, the first exodus's miracle quoted as the second exodus's weather report. And over the departing procession the book hangs its refrain like a border sign, the sentence that will close the entire volume: “There is no peace”, says the LORD, “for the wicked”. The comfort section of Isaiah is finished. What remains begins with a hand held out over the sea, and a mother who thinks God has forgotten her.

title: Inscribed on the Palms
subtitle: Isaiah 49
description: The Servant speaks for himself, Zion's name is found inscribed on God's palms, and the student's song follows.
paragraphs: The Servant speaks now in his own voice, addressing the whole map: “Listen to Me, O islands; pay attention, O distant peoples: The LORD called Me from the womb; from the body of My mother He named Me.” His equipment is weaponry worn in the mouth and the quiver: “He made My mouth like a sharp sword; He hid Me in the shadow of His hand. He made Me like a polished arrow; He hid Me in His quiver.” Sword and arrow, hidden in shadow and quiver, a weapon kept in reserve. And the commission as he reports it is the verse the retelling must not smooth, because the book itself does not: “You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory.” Israel is the name he is given, and the mission he is then handed is the gathering of Israel, so the name and the nation stand in the same sentence without the text pausing to reconcile them, and the Servant's own first recorded emotion is failure: “I have labored in vain, I have spent My strength in futility and vanity; yet My vindication is with the LORD, and My reward is with My God.” Spent strength, futility, vanity, and trust filed in the same breath. The answer to the failed laborer is an enlargement disguised as a rebuke of scale: “It is not enough for You to be My Servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the protected ones of Israel. I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth.” Too small a job, Jacob. The ends of the earth are added to the servant of rulers, to him “who was despised and abhorred by the nation, to the Servant of rulers”, and the reversal is scheduled in public: “Kings will see You and rise, and princes will bow down, because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen You.”

His covenant office from chapter forty-two is reissued with the prison work spelled out: kept and appointed as a covenant for the people, to restore the land and apportion its desolate inheritances, to say to the prisoners, come out, and to those in darkness, “Show yourselves”. And the released move through a tended landscape rather than a desert of escape: “They will feed along the pathways, and find pasture on every barren hill.” “They will not hunger or thirst, nor will scorching heat or sun beat down on them.” Compassion guides them beside springs of water, mountains are turned into roads, highways raised up, and the returnees converge from far away, north and west and the land of Aswan, until heaven and earth and mountains are ordered to break forth singing, for the LORD has comforted His people and will have compassion on His afflicted ones. And at that exact summit Zion objects, in the two sentences the whole chapter exists to answer: “The LORD has forsaken me; the Lord has forgotten me!” The answer is drawn from the nursery, and it concedes the impossible before it outbids it: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, or lack compassion for the son of her womb? Even if she could forget, I will not forget you!” Forsaken, she said; forgotten, she said; and the refutation is not an argument but a body part and an inscription: “Behold, I have inscribed you on the palms of My hands; your walls are ever before Me.” Palms: the working surface, looked at all day. Her builders hasten back while her wreckers depart; the children she thought dead arrive in such numbers that she wears them: “you will wear them all as jewelry and put them on like a bride”. The ruined places become too small, and the children of her bereavement say it in her hearing: “This place is too small for us; make room for us to live here.” And Zion, barren and exiled and rejected, does the arithmetic aloud in wonder: who begot these for me, who reared them, I was left all alone, so where did they come from?

The nations answer by carrying them: “Behold, I will lift up My hand to the nations, and raise My banner to the peoples. They will bring your sons in their arms and carry your daughters on their shoulders.” “Kings will be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers.” Kings facedown in the dust at her feet, and the knowledge formula seals it: “Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who hope in Me will never be put to shame.” The legal objection gets its hearing last: can plunder be snatched from the mighty, can a tyrant's captives be delivered? “Even the captives of the mighty will be taken away, and the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved; I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children.” Her oppressors eat their own flesh and drink their own blood like wine, “Then all mankind will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.” Chapter fifty opens with God's paperwork demanded in return: “Where is your mother’s certificate of divorce with which I sent her away? Or to which of My creditors did I sell you? Look, you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away.” No divorce certificate exists because no divorce occurred; the separation's cause is filed where it belongs, and the forsakenness Zion feels is answered with an empty file drawer. His absence had a different cause than rejection: “Why was no one there when I arrived? Why did no one answer when I called? Is My hand too short to redeem you? Or do I lack the strength to deliver you?”

Then the Servant speaks again, in the third of his songs, and his portrait is a student's: “The Lord GOD has given Me the tongue of discipleship, to sustain the weary with a word. He awakens Me morning by morning; He awakens My ear to listen as a disciple.” The Lord GOD has opened my ears, and I have not been rebellious, nor have I turned back. Not rebellious: Israel's defining sin named by its absence, in the Servant's obedience file, and the obedience's cost is reported without adornment: “I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle.” Back, cheeks, beard, spittle: the suffering is anatomized and the sufferer is not rescued inside the song. His confidence is juridical instead: “Because the Lord GOD helps Me, I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set My face like flint, and I know that I will not be put to shame.” “The One who vindicates Me is near. Who will dare to contend with Me? Let us confront each other!” Face set like flint: the flint is Isaiah's own country rock, and the song ends by sorting the audience into two kinds of fire-keepers: whoever fears the LORD and obeys the Servant's voice, walking in darkness without light, is told his doctrine: “Let him trust in the name of the LORD; let him lean on his God.” And the fire-kindlers, who array themselves with their own firebrands and walk by their own sparks, receive the other inheritance, and it is pronounced flatly: you will lie down in a place of torment. The Servant's school keeps both rolls. The next song opens on a shore, with a whole coastline ordered to listen and wait.

title: How Beautiful on the Mountains
subtitle: Isaiah 51
description: Three Listens, the cup of wrath lifted from Jerusalem, and beautiful feet on the mountains.
paragraphs: Listen to Me, the chapter commands, three times running, to three audiences in one people, and the first audience is told to study its own geology: “Listen to Me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: Look to the rock from which you were cut, and to the quarry from which you were hewn.” “Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth. When I called him, he was but one; then I blessed him and multiplied him.” Abraham, one man, counted by the book as the proof that small numbers are not the obstacle: the God who multiplied the one will repeat the operation on the remnant, and the evidence is the quarry itself. The promise for the ruins follows the pedigree immediately: “For the LORD will comfort Zion and will look with compassion on all her ruins; He will make her wilderness like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD.” Eden, the first garden, as the landscaping plan for the exile: joy and gladness found in her, thanksgiving and melodious song. The second Listen widens the audience past Zion's walls: “for a law will go out from Me, and My justice will become a light to the nations”, the Servant's light-to-the-nations office restated as a light going out from God's own law, and the schedule is impatient: “My righteousness draws near, My salvation is on the way, and My arms will bring justice to the nations. The islands will look for Me and wait in hope for My arm.” The islands wait for an arm; the book keeps personifying the rescue as a limb, and the limb is on its way.

The scale argument of chapter forty returns in the third Listen, now as consolation for insulted people: “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth below; for the heavens will vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and its people will die like gnats. But My salvation will last forever, and My righteousness will never fail.” Heavens smoke, earth a worn-out coat, people gnats: against that depreciation table one asset never declines. So: “Listen to Me, you who know what is right, you people with My law in your hearts: Do not fear the scorn of men; do not be broken by their insults.” The moth will devour the insulters like a garment and the worm will eat them like wool, garments eating their wearers in the same chapter where the earth is a garment God wears out. And then the congregation does something the book has trained it to do, it prays backward, seizing the arm doctrine and shaking it at heaven: “Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD. Wake up as in days past, as in generations of old. Was it not You who cut Rahab to pieces, who pierced through the dragon?” “Was it not You who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over?” Rahab, Egypt's nickname from chapter thirty, cut to pieces: the exiles weaponize the exodus in prayer, and the prayer's answer is quoted from the road song itself, chapter thirty-five's refrain returning as a guarantee: “So the redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.”

God's reply opens with the comfort formula at full strength: “I, even I, am He who comforts you. Why should you be afraid of mortal man, of a son of man who withers like grass?” You have forgotten the LORD, your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the earth's foundations, and you live in terror all day long of an oppressor whose fury is about to become unfindable: where is the fury of the oppressor? “The captive will soon be freed; he will not die in the dungeon, and his bread will not be lacking.” My words, the Creator says, are in your mouth, and you are covered with the shadow of My hand, the cosmos re-founded for a single sentence: to say to Zion, You are My people. And then the cup is addressed, the book's most brutal tableware, passed to Jerusalem to drink: “Awake, awake! Rise up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of His fury; you who have drained the goblet to the dregs”, the cup that makes men stagger, drained by a city with no son left to guide her or take her hand, her boys fainted at every street head like antelopes in a net, full of the wrath of the LORD. Hear this, you afflicted one, drunken but not with wine: the cup has an itinerary, and Jerusalem is not its last stop: “See, I have removed from your hand the cup of staggering. From that goblet, the cup of My fury, you will never drink again.” “I will place it in the hands of your tormentors”, the ones who made a street of her back: “Lie down, so we can walk over you”. The cup of staggering changes hands in the text's own fingers, from the daughter to her tormentors, and the street they walked over becomes the road home.

Chapter fifty-two calls the awakening for the city herself: “Awake, awake, clothe yourself with strength, O Zion! Put on your garments of splendor, O Jerusalem, holy city!” “Shake off your dust! Rise up and sit on your throne, O Jerusalem. Remove the chains from your neck, O captive Daughter of Zion.” Dust, the taunt-song address of Babylon in chapter forty-seven, is now shaken off Zion's own shoulders; the ground she sat on without a throne is vacated for a throne. The economics of her rescue are stated as an insult to her captors: “You were sold for nothing, and without money you will be redeemed.” Egypt took them down long ago, Assyria oppressed without cause, Babylon rules them and blasphemes God's name continually all day long, and the deliverance is scheduled as a lesson in a name: “Therefore My people will know My name; therefore they will know on that day that I am He who speaks. Here I am!” Then the mountains get the book's most beautiful sentence, about feet: “How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news, who proclaim peace, who bring good tidings, who proclaim salvation”, messengers whose whole message compresses into the announcement they make to Zion: “Your God reigns!” “Listen!
