Your watchmen lift up their voices, together they shout for joy. For every eye will see when the LORD returns to Zion.” Watchmen shouting, plural voices in unison, the watchtower of chapter twenty-one relieved at last; the ruins themselves are ordered to sing in chorus: “Break forth in joy, sing together, O ruins of Jerusalem, for the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem.” “The LORD has bared His holy arm in the sight of all the nations; all the ends of the earth will see the salvation of our God.” The departure orders follow in priestly language, the exodus run as a procession instead of an escape: “Depart, depart, go out from there! Touch no unclean thing; come out from it, purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD.” “For you will not leave in a hurry nor flee in haste, for the LORD goes before you, and the God of Israel is your rear guard.” Not in a hurry: the first exodus left by night with dough unbaked; this one walks, vanguard and rearguard both God. And on the procession's edge the book sets the doorway to its greatest chapter, the Servant exalted and disfigured in a single breath: “Behold, My Servant will prosper; He will be raised and lifted up and highly exalted.” “Just as many were appalled at Him”, “His appearance was disfigured beyond that of any man, and His form was marred beyond human likeness”, “so He will sprinkle many nations. Kings will shut their mouths because of Him. For they will see what they have not been told, and they will understand what they have not heard.” The doorway opens. The next episode walks through it and does not look away.

title: By His Stripes
subtitle: Isaiah 53
description: The suffering Servant, nearly whole; then the barren woman sings and the market opens free.
paragraphs: “Who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?” The fourth song of the Servant opens as a report nobody credited, and then tells the story in the first person plural, we, the confessors narrating their own misjudgment as the song's substance. “He grew up before Him like a tender shoot, and like a root out of dry ground. He had no stately form or majesty to attract us, no beauty that we should desire Him.” A shoot again, the book's stump botany, this time out of dry ground, unmajestic, undesirable. “He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief. Like one from whom men hide their faces, He was despised, and we esteemed Him not.” Esteemed Him not: the evaluation is confessed as the speakers' error, and the correction of the error is the chapter's engine: “Surely He took up our infirmities and carried our sorrows; yet we considered Him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted.” We considered Him stricken by God, and the considering was wrong, because the striking had a different ledger entirely: “But He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him, and by His stripes we are healed.” Pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities, the prepositions do the theology, and the confession generalizes itself before it can be mistaken for someone else's autobiography: “We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way; and the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all.” All, each, us all: the flock's whole record, laid by the LORD's own hand on the one figure in the song who is never said to have strayed.

His conduct under the laying-on is the silence the earlier songs prepared: “He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth. He was led like a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth.” The man whose mouth was a sharp sword in chapter forty-nine does not open it here; the tongue of discipleship from chapter fifty sustains the weary with a word and offers none in self-defense. “By oppression and judgment He was taken away, and who can recount His descendants? For He was cut off from the land of the living; He was stricken for the transgression of My people.” Cut off, descendant-less, the genealogy closed by violence and verdict together. “He was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death, although He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth.” Grave assignments, plural indignity and single honor in one sentence, over a man whose innocence is stated as a matter of record: no violence done, no deceit spoken. And then the song says the hardest sentence in the book, about the willing of it: “Yet it was the LORD’s will to crush Him and to cause Him to suffer; and when His soul is made a guilt offering, He will see His offspring, He will prolong His days, and the good pleasure of the LORD will prosper in His hand.” A guilt offering, the Levitical category for restitution, made of a soul: and on the far side of it, offspring for the descendant-less, days prolonged for the cut off, prosperity for the crushed. “After the anguish of His soul, He will see the light of life and be satisfied. By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities.” Justify many: the courtroom verb of the whole section, discharged at last by knowledge and bearing. “Therefore I will allot Him a portion with the great, and He will divide the spoils with the strong, because He has poured out His life unto death, and He was numbered with the transgressors. Yet He bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.” Spoils divided with the strong by the man who poured out his life unto death; intercession made by the silent one, for the transgressors, at the end. The song is twelve verses long and the retelling adds nothing to it, because there is nothing in it that addition would improve; it is left standing the way the book leaves it, a doorway chapter fifty-two opened and a room no summary furnishes better than its own words.

Chapter fifty-four answers the song with a wedding and a building program, addressed to the barren woman of the forsakenness complaint: “Shout for joy, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth in song and cry aloud, you who have never travailed; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband”. The tent is to be enlarged before the children arrive: “Enlarge the site of your tent, stretch out the curtains of your dwellings, do not hold back. Lengthen your ropes and drive your stakes in deep.” The shame of her youth and the reproach of her widowhood are scheduled for forgetting, because the relationship is re-founded on the identity of the husband: “For your husband is your Maker”, “the LORD of Hosts is His name”, “the Holy One of Israel is your Redeemer; He is called the God of all the earth.” Called back like a wife deserted and wounded in spirit, like the rejected wife of one's youth, she hears the marriage's whole crisis re-measured by its Maker: “For a brief moment I forsook you, but with great compassion I will bring you back.” “In a surge of anger I hid My face from you for a moment, but with everlasting kindness I will have compassion on you”. A brief moment against everlasting, and the oath is filed under Noah: as the waters will never again cover the earth, so the anger will not return; and geology itself is offered as the weaker covenant partner: “Though the mountains may be removed and the hills may be shaken, My loving devotion will not depart from you, and My covenant of peace will not be broken”. The afflicted city, lashed by storms and without solace, is rebuilt in jewelry: “O afflicted city, lashed by storms, without solace, surely I will set your stones in antimony and lay your foundations with sapphires.” Pinnacles of rubies, gates of sparkling jewels, walls of precious stones, and the curriculum of her children guaranteed at the source: “Then all your sons will be taught by the LORD, and great will be their prosperity.” The chapter closes by arming her with her Maker's monopoly: He created the craftsman who forges the weapon and the destroyer who wields it, so the heritage of the LORD's servants is announced as the movement's security doctrine: “No weapon formed against you shall prosper, and you will refute every tongue that accuses you. This is the heritage of the servants of the LORD, and their vindication is from Me”. Servants, plural now: the Servant's heritage, distributed.

Chapter fifty-five opens the market: “Come, all you who are thirsty, come to the waters; and you without money, come, buy, and eat! Come, buy wine and milk without money and without cost!” The economics are an interrogation: “Why spend money on that which is not bread, and your labor on that which does not satisfy? Listen carefully to Me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in the richest of foods.” “Incline your ear and come to Me; listen, so that your soul may live.” “I will make with you an everlasting covenant”, the loving devotion promised to David, transferred from the dynasty to the thirsty, and the summoned nations will run to a people glorified by the Holy One of Israel. The invitation carries an expiry and a pardon in the same breath: “Seek the LORD while He may be found; call on Him while He is near.” “Let the wicked man forsake his way and the unrighteous man his thoughts; let him return to the LORD, that He may have compassion, and to our God, for He will freely pardon.” And the pardon is defended by the book's epistemology, the declaration that explains every overturned expectation in Isaiah, the aqueduct, the stump, the song: “For My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways”. “For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so My ways are higher than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts.” Rain and snow do not return to heaven unspent; they water, bud, sprout, seed and bread follow; “so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please, and it will prosper where I send it.” The word's irrigation record is perfect. And the movement ends in procession music, the redeemed going out the way chapter fifty-two prescribed, neither hurrying nor fleeing, escorted by a landscape converted into an orchestra: “You will indeed go out with joy and be led forth in peace; the mountains and hills will burst into song before you, and all the trees of the field will clap their hands.” “Instead of the thornbush, the cypress will grow, and instead of the brier, the myrtle will spring up; this will make a name for the LORD, an everlasting sign, never to be destroyed.” Thornbush to cypress, Edom's briers to myrtle, the world replanted as a sign with no expiry. The comfort section is finished. What remains of the book is the argument about what the comfort costs and whom it includes, and it opens with a fast.

title: The Fast I Have Chosen
subtitle: Isaiah 56
description: Foreigners and eunuchs welcomed, watchmen asleep, and the fast God chose.
paragraphs: The book's last movement opens with ethics, dated to the edge of the arrival: “Maintain justice and do what is right, for My salvation is coming soon, and My righteousness will be revealed.” The beatitude that follows is occupational: “Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds it fast, who keeps the Sabbath without profaning it and keeps his hand from doing any evil.” And then the doors are thrown open in both directions the old order kept them shut, to the foreigner and to the eunuch, the two people the assembly's rules most thoroughly excluded. The foreigner who has joined himself to the LORD is forbidden his own despair: “The LORD will utterly exclude me from His people”, he is not to say; and the eunuch, a man with no descendants and no future in any registry, is forbidden his: “I am but a dry tree.” A dry tree, in the book of the stump and the shoot, is a loaded metaphor, and God's counter-offer to the childless man is the Servant's own arithmetic: keep My Sabbaths, choose what pleases Me, hold fast to My covenant, and “I will give them, in My house and within My walls, a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters. I will give them an everlasting name that will not be cut off.” Better than sons and daughters, an everlasting name that will not be cut off, for the man whose name was scheduled to end with him: the reversed cut-off of chapter fifty-three, inheritance without genealogy. The foreigners who join themselves to the LORD get the mountain itself: “I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in My house of prayer. Their burnt offerings and sacrifices will be accepted on My altar, for My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations.” And the Gatherer's summary leaves the door visibly wider than the gathering: “I will gather to them still others besides those already gathered.”

Then the beasts are invited to the field the watchmen have abandoned, and the shepherds of the post-exile community get the book's last animal satire: “Israel’s watchmen are blind, they are all oblivious; they are all mute dogs, they cannot bark; they are dreamers lying around, loving to slumber.” Watchmen who cannot bark, shepherds with no discernment, ravenous dogs never satisfied, each turned to his own way and his own gain, and their forward planning is quoted as a toast: “Come, let me get the wine, let us imbibe the strong drink, and tomorrow will be like today, only far better!” Chapter fifty-seven opens on the other end of the community, the deaths nobody mourns: “The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart; devout men are taken away, while no one considers that the righteous are taken away from the presence of evil.” “Those who walk uprightly enter into peace; they find rest, lying down in death.” The taken-away righteous are the fortunate ones, spared the neighborhood the chapter then tours at full strength and without abbreviation: sons of a sorceress, offspring of adulterers, lust burned among the oaks and under every green tree, children slaughtered in the valleys under the clefts of the rocks, drink offerings poured to the smooth stones of the wadi, beds made on high and lofty hills and behind the door and the doorpost, envoys sent a great distance, down even to Sheol, for Molech's oil and perfumes. Wearied by the many journeys and still not saying there is no hope: religion as an addiction that renews its own strength. And God's analysis of the apostasy is psychological in one question: whom have you dreaded and feared, that you lied and did not remember Me; is it because I have long been silent that you do not fear Me? The silent years of chapter forty-two, read from below as permission. His remedy is exposure with an exit: I will expose your righteousness and your works, and they will not profit you; when you cry out, let your companies of idols deliver you, the wind will carry them off, a breath will take them away; “But he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain.”

The highway crew is then ordered out one more time: “Build it up, build it up, prepare the way, take every obstacle out of the way of My people.” And the high and lifted up One, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy, states His two addresses in the sentence that holds the whole book's altitude: “I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly and revive the heart of the contrite.” High and holy, and with the crushed: both residences, one God, the second kept for reviving purposes. “For I will not accuse you forever, nor will I always be angry”, for the spirit of man would faint before the Maker of the breath of life. The backslider is audited without mercy and healed without condition: I was enraged by his sinful greed; I struck him and hid My face in anger; yet he kept turning back to the desires of his heart. “I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will guide him and restore comfort to him and his mourners”, bringing praise to lips that have not managed it, “Peace, peace to those far and near”, “and I will heal them”. And over the other party hangs the border sign from chapter forty-eight, now with my God in the attribution: “But the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck.” “There is no peace”, says my God, “for the wicked”.

Chapter fifty-eight stages the movement's central confrontation, and it starts with volume: “Cry aloud, do not hold back! Raise your voice like a ram’s horn. Declare to My people their transgression and to the house of Jacob their sins.” The people under indictment are, by the text's own account, keenly religious: day after day they seek God and delight to know His ways, like a nation that does what is right; they ask for righteous judgments and delight in the nearness of God; and their complaint against heaven is a customer's complaint: “Why have we fasted, and You have not seen? Why have we humbled ourselves, and You have not noticed?” The answer is an audit of the fast day itself: behold, on the day of your fast you do as you please and you oppress all your workers. “You fast with contention and strife to strike viciously with your fist. You cannot fast as you do today and have your voice be heard on high.” “Is this the fast I have chosen: a day for a man to deny himself, to bow his head like a reed, and to spread out sackcloth and ashes? Will you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the LORD?” The reed-bowed head and the ash bedding are described precisely in order to be rejected as the definition, and then the definition is given, twice, in the book's clearest ethical prose: “Isn’t this the fast that I have chosen: to break the chains of wickedness, to untie the cords of the yoke, to set the oppressed free and tear off every yoke?” “Isn’t it to share your bread with the hungry, to bring the poor and homeless into your home, to clothe the naked when you see him, and not to turn away from your own flesh and blood?” Chains, yokes, bread, a roof, clothing: chapter one's syllabus, defended at last as liturgy. Do this fast, and the light economics invert themselves: “Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will come quickly. Your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the LORD will be your rear guard.” Rear guard, the exodus pillar stationed behind the procession of chapter fifty-two, reissued as the bodyguard of the bread-sharers. “Then you will call, and the LORD will answer; you will cry out”, and He will say He is here, the Here I am of chapter fifty-two's God, transferred to the call of the fasting righteous. Remove the yoke and the pointing finger and the malicious talk, “and if you give yourself to the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, then your light will go forth in the darkness, and your night will be like noonday.” “The LORD will always guide you; He will satisfy you in a sun-scorched land and strengthen your frame. You will be like a well-watered garden, like a spring whose waters never fail.” And the work description of the fasting people turns out to be the city's: “Your people will rebuild the ancient ruins; you will restore the age-old foundations; you will be called Repairer of the Breach, Restorer of the Streets of Dwelling.” The Sabbath closes the chapter the way it opened the movement, delight rather than burden, heritage rather than deprivation: ride on the heights of the land, fed with the heritage of Jacob, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken. The fast God chose feeds other people. The next chapter opens in a darkened room, with the people asking why the light has not come.

title: Arise, Shine
subtitle: Isaiah 59
description: Confession in the dark, then sunrise: arise, shine, for your light has come.
paragraphs: The dark chapter begins by acquitting the machinery: “Surely the arm of the LORD is not too short to save, nor His ear too dull to hear.” Chapter fifty's question, is My hand too short to redeem, is answered as a premise: the arm and the ear are fine. “But your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you, so that He does not hear.” The barrier is itemized body part by body part, an anatomy of the obstacle course: “For your hands are stained with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken lies, and your tongue mutters injustice.” Hands of chapter one's prayer again, covered with blood and still spread out. The courts are dead, no one calls for justice or pleads honestly, empty pleas and lies, mischief conceived and iniquity birthed like Hosea's labor ward, viper eggs hatched and spider webs woven that cannot clothe anyone, feet running to evil and swift to shed innocent blood, and the way of peace unknown: their roads are crooked by design, so no one treading them knows peace, the refrain's negative stated as a road condition. And the chapter's speakers are the people themselves, confessing in chorus: “Therefore justice is far from us, and righteousness does not reach us. We hope for light, but there is darkness; for brightness, but we walk in gloom.” “Like the blind, we feel our way along the wall, groping like those without eyes. We stumble at midday as in the twilight; among the vigorous we are like the dead.” “We all growl like bears and moan like doves. We hope for justice, but find none, for salvation, but it is far from us.”

The confession is itemized as carefully as the indictment: “For our transgressions are multiplied before You, and our sins testify against us.” “rebelling and denying the LORD, turning away from our God, speaking oppression and revolt, conceiving and uttering lies from the heart”, the whole file read aloud by its defendants. And the civic consequence is drawn in one of the book's saddest street scenes: “So justice is turned away, and righteousness stands at a distance. For truth has stumbled in the public square, and honesty cannot enter.” Truth is missing; whoever turns from evil becomes prey; and the divine response is not yet anger, it is inventory: the LORD looked and was displeased that there was no justice. “He saw that there was no man; He was amazed that there was no one to intercede. So His own arm brought salvation, and His own righteousness sustained Him.” No man, no intercessor, the intercession gap the Servant's song answered is here answered by armor: “He put on righteousness like a breastplate, and the helmet of salvation on His head; He put on garments of vengeance and wrapped Himself in a cloak of zeal.” God's own arm, dressed for the campaign His people's confession admitted no one else could fight: repayment to enemies and islands alike, His name feared from sunset to sunrise, His coming like a raging flood driven by His own breath. And the covenant that survives the flood is specified to the turning remnant: “The Redeemer will come to Zion, to those in Jacob who turn from transgression”. “My Spirit will not depart from you, and My words that I have put in your mouth will not depart from your mouth or from the mouths of your children and grandchildren, from now on and forevermore”. The book's own transmission is covenanted inside its second-to-last movement: the words stay in the mouths, mouth to mouth, grandchildren deep, forevermore.

Chapter sixty is the sunrise the confession was groping for, and it opens with the imperative the whole book has been walking toward: “Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the LORD rises upon you.” “For behold, darkness covers the earth, and thick darkness is over the peoples; but the LORD will rise upon you, and His glory will appear over you.” “Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn.” Chapter two's stream of nations, arriving at last, and the procession's cargo is the children: sons from afar, daughters carried on the arm, the mother of chapter forty-nine wearing them as jewelry now by the shipload. The wealth of the sea and the riches of the nations pour in behind them, camel caravans covering the land: “Caravans of camels will cover your land, young camels of Midian and Ephah, and all from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD.” Kedar's flocks and Nebaioth's rams ascend the altar with acceptance, foreigners rebuild the walls and kings serve, the gates stand open day and night because the traffic never stops: “Your gates will always stand open; they will never be shut, day or night, so that the wealth of the nations may be brought into you, with their kings being led in procession.” The nations that will not serve will perish, the chapter concedes, and then returns to the reversal it prefers: “Who are these who fly like clouds, like doves to their shelters?” “The sons of your oppressors will come and bow down to you; all who reviled you will fall facedown at your feet and call you the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel.” Forsaken and despised and walked past no longer, she will nurse at the breasts of royalty and learn the lesson by drinking it: “you will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob”.

The city's upgrade is metallurgical and constitutional in the same breath: “Instead of bronze I will bring you gold; I will bring silver in place of iron, bronze instead of wood, and iron instead of stones. I will appoint peace as your governor and righteousness as your ruler.” Peace the governor, righteousness the overseer, an administration staffed by abstractions made literal. “No longer will violence be heard in your land, nor ruin or destruction within your borders. But you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise.” And the luminaries retire: “No longer will the sun be your light by day, nor the brightness of the moon shine on your night; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor.” “Your sun will no longer set, and your moon will not wane; for the LORD will be your everlasting light, and the days of your sorrow will cease.” The chapter of darkness in chapter twenty-four, where the moon was confounded and the sun ashamed, is answered by a city that has replaced both lights with a Person. The population clause is the movement's most sweeping predicate: “Then all your people will be righteous; they will possess the land forever; they are the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, so that I may be glorified.” The branch of My planting, the shoot become a nation, God's own horticulture for His own glory. And the least is given the census of the kingdom: “The least of you will become a thousand, and the smallest a mighty nation. I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly.” In its time, quickly: the timetable paradox the whole book runs on, spoken over a city still sitting in chapter fifty-nine's gloom. The next chapter anoints a preacher for the interval, and gives him his text.

title: The Year of the LORD's Favor
subtitle: Isaiah 61
description: The year of the LORD's favor, watchmen who never keep silent, and a city with new names.
paragraphs: “The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and freedom to the prisoners”, “to proclaim the year of the LORD’s favor and the day of our God’s vengeance, to comfort all who mourn”. An anointed preacher speaks in the first person at the head of the book's last movement, and his commission reads like the index of everything Isaiah has promised: good news to the poor, the book's oldest constituency; binding for the brokenhearted; liberty and freedom for the captives the Servant's covenant office named; the year of favor and the day of vengeance held in one proclamation, comfort for the mourners scheduled alongside. His work among the mourners of Zion is an exchange of wardrobe: “to give them a crown of beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, and a garment of praise for a spirit of despair.” Ashes off, crown on; mourning traded for oil, despair for a garment, and the re-clothed mourners receive the book's final piece of tree language, the stump series ending in timber: “So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the LORD, that He may be glorified.” Oaks of righteousness, planted by the LORD himself: the terebinth stump of chapter six, grown at last into a grove with a name. Their employment is construction: “They will rebuild the ancient ruins; they will restore the places long devastated; they will renew the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations.” Strangers will feed their flocks and work their fields, and their own title is the priesthood the whole nation was once promised at Sinai, now spoken over the mourners: “But you will be called the priests of the LORD; they will speak of you as ministers of our God; you will feed on the wealth of nations, and you will boast in their riches.”

The shame account is settled in the exile's own currency, double: “Instead of shame, My people will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation, they will rejoice in their share; and so they will inherit a double portion in their land, and everlasting joy will be theirs.” Double for all her sins, Jerusalem heard at the comfort's opening; double portion, her children hear at its climax, the arithmetic reversed on the same word. The covenant underwriting it is stated as a character reference: “For I, the LORD, love justice; I hate robbery and iniquity; in My faithfulness I will give them their recompense and make an everlasting covenant with them.” Their descendants will be known among the nations as a people the LORD has blessed on sight. And the chapter's last voice is the bride's, rejoicing in the first person about the clothes: “I will rejoice greatly in the LORD, my soul will exult in my God; for He has clothed me with garments of salvation and wrapped me in a robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom wears a priestly headdress, as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.” Garments of salvation, a robe of righteousness, the wardrobe of chapter sixty-one issued and worn. The ground itself guarantees the growth: “For as the earth brings forth its growth, and as a garden enables seed to spring up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to spring up before all the nations.”

Chapter sixty-two opens with a vow of insomnia, and the vow is God's watchman speaking, or the prophet, or the anointed; the book lets the voice stand for all three at once: “For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not keep still, until her righteousness shines like a bright light, her salvation like a blazing torch.” “Nations will see your righteousness, and all kings your glory. You will be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will bestow.” “You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the LORD, a royal diadem in the palm of your God.” A crown in the hand, the drunk crown of chapter twenty-eight answered by a sober one held by God himself. And the renaming is the chapter's sacrament, the forsakenness complaint of chapter forty-nine answered with registry entries: “No longer will you be called Forsaken, nor your land named Desolate; but you will be called Hephzibah, and your land Beulah; for the LORD will take delight in you, and your land will be His bride.” Hephzibah, My delight is in her; Beulah, Married: the land a bride, and the bridegroom's joy made the measure of heaven's: “as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you”. Her sons will marry her, the text startles by saying, the citizens wedded to their own city, and God's rejoicing over her is the chapter's loudest note. The watchmen are then posted with instructions that turn prayer into a siege of heaven: “On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have posted watchmen; they will never be silent day or night.” You who call on the LORD, take no rest for yourselves, “nor give Him any rest until He establishes Jerusalem and makes her the praise of the earth”. No rest for the intercessors, no rest for God: chapter fifty-nine's missing intercessor has become a wall full of them, and their job description is holy nagging until the praise of the earth is established.

The oath that backs the watchmen is sworn by God's right hand and mighty arm, and its content is a farm bill, food security as a covenant clause: “Never again will I give your grain to your enemies for food, nor will foreigners drink the new wine for which you have toiled.” Those who harvest will eat it and praise the LORD; those who gather will drink in His holy courts. And the highway crew goes out one final time, at the movement's end as at its beginning, banners raised for the nations: “Go out, go out through the gates; prepare the way for the people! Build it up, build up the highway; clear away the stones; raise a banner for the nations!” The proclamation runs to the ends of the earth, and it is chapter forty's arrival notice, matured into a name and a payroll: “Say to Daughter Zion: See, your Savior comes! Look, His reward is with Him, and His recompense goes before Him.” And the final registry entries close the chapter like seals: “And they will be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of The LORD; and you will be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.” Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken: the exact reverse of chapter forty-nine's complaint, entered now as her legal name. The book's last movement has two chapters of weather left, winepress and judgment, and then the new heavens. The next voice heard is God's own, pleading to be found by people who never asked for Him.

title: Rend the Heavens
subtitle: Isaiah 63
description: The warrior comes from Edom alone, and the book's longest prayer remembers everything.
paragraphs: The book's last dialogue opens as a sentry's challenge, addressed to a figure approaching from the south, from Edom, from Bozrah, in spattered clothes: “Who is this coming from Edom, from Bozrah with crimson-stained garments? Who is this robed in splendor, marching in the greatness of His strength?” “It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save.” Why are Your clothes red, like one who treads the winepress? And the answer is the winepress chapter of chapter thirty-four, reported in the first person by the Treader himself: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no one from the nations was with Me. I trampled them in My anger and trod them down in My fury; their blood spattered My garments, and all My clothes were stained.” “For the day of vengeance was in My heart, and the year of My redemption had come.” The day of vengeance and the year of redemption are the same season in the Treader's calendar, the year of the LORD's favor's other face. “I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled that no one assisted. So My arm brought Me salvation, and My own wrath upheld Me.” No one to help: chapter fifty-nine's appraisal exactly, there was no man and no intercessor, and the arm that saved Israel alone in the armor chapter saves its Owner here, upholding Him in the press. I trampled the nations in My anger; in My wrath I made them drunk and poured out their blood on the ground: the cup of staggering's last serving, poured out on the earth itself by the hand that once passed it to Jerusalem. Edom, the burden section's exhibit, receives its full sentence offstage between the songs, and the watchman's report of it is six verses long and entirely arterial.

Then the voice changes entirely, and the book's longest act of corporate memory begins, a psalm of the community recounting kindnesses like a family going through an album backward: “I will make known the LORD’s loving devotion and His praiseworthy acts, because of all that the LORD has done for us”, the many good things for the house of Israel according to His great compassion. “They are surely My people, sons who will not be disloyal.” “So He became their Savior.” “In all their distress, He too was afflicted, and the Angel of His Presence saved them. In His love and compassion He redeemed them; He lifted them up and carried them all the days of old.” Carried, the chapter forty-six transport doctrine in the past tense: the carrying God carried them then. “But they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit. So He turned and became their enemy, and He Himself fought against them.” Grieved His Holy Spirit: the rebellion is diagnosed as a grief inflicted, and the war that followed was fought by God against His own carried children. Then His people remembered the days of old, the days of Moses, and the memory turns interrogative, the Where is He liturgy: “Where is He who brought them through the sea with the shepherds of His flock? Where is the One who set His Holy Spirit among them”, who sent His glorious arm by Moses' right hand, divided the waters for everlasting renown, led them through the depths like a horse in the wilderness so they did not stumble. Like cattle going down to the valley, the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest: You led Your people this way to make for Yourself a glorious name. The memory is an argument, and the argument is aimed upward: “Look down from heaven and see, from Your holy and glorious habitation. Where are Your zeal and might? Your yearning and compassion for me are restrained.” Restrained, the charge Hezekiah once feared about himself inverted against heaven: God holding back His own compassion is the prayer's problem. “Yet You are our Father, though Abraham does not know us and Israel does not acknowledge us. You, O LORD, are our Father; our Redeemer from Everlasting is Your name.” Abraham and Israel, the patriarchs themselves, disclaimed as insufficient sponsors: the prayer goes over their heads to the Fatherhood behind them, Redeemer from Everlasting, the title of chapter forty-one's worm speech.

And the prayer does not stop at praise; it cross-examines: “Why, O LORD, do You make us stray from Your ways and harden our hearts from fearing You? Return, for the sake of Your servants, the tribes of Your heritage.” Our enemies have trampled Your sanctuary; for a short while Your people possessed Your holy place; we have become like those You never ruled, like those not called by Your name. Chapter sixty-four is the demand that follows, the book's most violent prayer request, a request for theophany as artillery: “If only You would rend the heavens and come down, so that mountains would quake at Your presence”, as fire kindles brushwood and boils water, to make Your name known to Your enemies, so that the nations will tremble at Your presence. The historical exhibits are entered: when You did awesome works we did not expect, You came down and the mountains trembled. And the uniqueness clause is stated as the warrant for the whole procedure: “From ancient times no one has heard, no ear has perceived, no eye has seen any God besides You, who acts on behalf of those who wait for Him.” Those who wait for Him: the waiting doctrine in the mouth of the demanders, asking the God of the waiters to hurry. “You welcome those who gladly do right, who remember Your ways. Surely You were angry, for we sinned.” “How can we be saved if we remain in our sins?” The confession that follows is the book's most quoted self-assessment and needs no improvement from a reteller: “Each of us has become like something unclean, and all our righteous acts are like filthy rags; we all wither like a leaf, and our iniquities carry us away like the wind.” All our righteous acts: the fasting of chapter fifty-eight and the seeking of chapter fifty-eight, weighed by their own owners and found to be rags. “No one calls on Your name or strives to take hold of You. For You have hidden Your face from us and delivered us into the hand of our iniquity.” Delivered into the hand of our iniquity, as into a captor's custody: the sin as jailer. And then the potter doctrine of the Egypt chapters is picked up by the clay itself and used as a prayer: “But now, O LORD, You are our Father; we are the clay, and You are the potter; we are all the work of Your hand.” The clay that was warned not to quarrel with its Maker now pleads its Maker's workmanship as its defense. “Do not be angry, O LORD, beyond measure; do not remember our iniquity forever. Oh, look upon us, we pray; we are all Your people!” The evidence closes with the ruins, holy cities a wilderness, Zion a wasteland, Jerusalem a desolation: “Our holy and beautiful temple, where our fathers praised You, has been burned with fire, and all that was dear to us lies in ruins.” “After all this, O LORD, will You restrain Yourself? Will You keep silent and afflict us beyond measure?” The prayer ends there, unanswered inside its own chapter, the silence of God its final line. The book's answer, when it comes in the next chapter, begins with God saying He let Himself be found by people who never asked.

title: New Heavens and a New Earth
subtitle: Isaiah 65
description: New heavens and a new earth; the book ends with worship and a sight the retelling will not soften.
paragraphs: God's answer to the great prayer opens with the complaint reversed: the nation that accused Him of hiding learns who was actually hiding from whom. “I revealed Myself to those who did not ask for Me; I was found by those who did not seek Me.” To a nation that did not call My name, I said, “Here I am! Here I am!” The Here I am of the answering God, doubled, spent on people who never asked. “All day long I have held out My hands to an obstinate people who walk in the wrong path, who follow their own imaginations”, a people provoking Him to His face in gardens and on brick altars, sitting among the graves, spending nights in secret places, eating the meat of pigs, and policing their own holiness against heaven itself: “Keep to yourself; do not come near me, for I am holier than you!” “Such people are smoke in My nostrils, a fire that burns all day long.” Behold, it is written before Me: I will not keep silent, but I will repay, into their laps, their iniquities and their fathers' together, full payment for the former deeds. And inside the repayment stands the sorter, with a grape cluster for his parable: as men spare a cluster because there is a blessing in it, “so I will act on behalf of My servants; I will not destroy them all”. “And I will bring forth descendants from Jacob, and heirs from Judah; My elect will possess My mountains, and My servants will dwell there.” “Sharon will become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a resting place for herds, for My people who seek Me.” Achor, the valley of trouble where the first conquest's theft was buried, re-zoned as a resting place: the geography of shame repastured for the seekers.

The other file is closed in the same chapter, with the refusal formula the whole book keeps sentencing: “I will destine you for the sword, and you will all kneel down to be slaughtered, because I called and you did not answer, I spoke and you did not listen; you did evil in My sight and chose that in which I did not delight.” The forsakers who set a table for Fortune and poured mixed wine for Destiny get their destinies from a different hand, and the contrast is drawn as a table service: “My servants will eat, but you will go hungry; My servants will drink, but you will go thirsty; My servants will rejoice, but you will be put to shame.” My servants will shout for joy with a glad heart, but you will cry out with a heavy heart and wail with a broken spirit. Your name becomes a curse invoked by My chosen ones; “but to His servants He will give another name”. By the God of truth will blessing and oath be sworn in that land, “For the former troubles will be forgotten and hidden from My sight.” And then the horizon the whole book has been bending toward opens at full width: “For behold, I will create new heavens and a new earth. The former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” “But be glad and rejoice forever in what I create; for I will create Jerusalem to be a joy and its people to be a delight.” “I will rejoice in Jerusalem and take delight in My people. The sounds of weeping and crying will no longer be heard in her.” The new creation's demographics are pastoral and long: “No longer will a nursing infant live but a few days, or an old man fail to live out his years. For the youth will die at a hundred years, and he who fails to reach a hundred will be considered accursed.” Death still exists in the picture, but demoted to a rarity at a hundred. “They will build houses and dwell in them; they will plant vineyards and eat their fruit.” The curse of building for others and planting for others, Deuteronomy's terror, is repealed clause by clause: “For as is the lifetime of a tree, so will be the days of My people, and My chosen ones will fully enjoy the work of their hands.” They will not labor in vain or bear children doomed to disaster. And prayer in that world runs on an anticipation circuit: “Even before they call, I will answer, and while they are still speaking, I will hear.” The chapter closes where chapter eleven opened, in the peaceable kingdom, with one tenant amended: “The wolf and the lamb will feed together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox, but the food of the serpent will be dust. They will neither harm nor destroy on all My holy mountain”. The serpent's diet is not reformed; it is Eden's sentence, left standing in Paradise. Everything else is fed.

The last chapter opens by downsizing the temple: “Heaven is My throne, and earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me? Or where will My place of repose be?” Has not My hand made all these things? The building committee is dismissed, and the esteem of God is assigned to posture rather than project: “This is the one I will esteem: he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word.” High and holy place, with the contrite: chapter fifty-seven's two addresses, now the book's official doctrine of address. The ritual murders are then read in their true equivalences, chapter one's sacrifice audit returned with the volume up: “Whoever slaughters an ox is like one who slays a man; whoever sacrifices a lamb is like one who breaks a dog’s neck”, grain offering as pig's blood, frankincense as idol blessing, because they chose their own ways and delighted in their abominations; so I will choose their punishment, since I called and no one answered, I spoke and no one listened. To the tremblers, by contrast, a word against their own brothers, the excluders who mock them in the name of piety: “Let the LORD be glorified that we may see your joy!” “But they will be put to shame.” Uproar from the city, a voice from the temple: the voice of the LORD repaying His enemies. And Zion's labor arrives backwards, birth before pain, a nation delivered in an instant: “Who has heard of such as this? Who has seen such things? Can a country be born in a day or a nation be delivered in an instant? Yet as soon as Zion was in labor, she gave birth to her children.” “Shall I bring a baby to the point of birth and not deliver it?” Hezekiah's birth-without-strength image, answered at the scale of a city: the God who delivers does not close the womb. The nursing mother returns at the scale of the metropolis: “I will extend peace to her like a river, and the wealth of nations like a flowing stream; you will nurse and be carried on her arm, and bounced upon her knees.” “As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you, and you will be consoled over Jerusalem.” Comfort, comfort My people: the book's first imperative, arriving as its last promise, delivered by the mothering God in person.

The ending widens and darkens in the same motion, and the retelling does not avert its eyes at the finish line any more than at the start. “For behold, the LORD will come with fire”, chariots like a whirlwind, anger executed with fury, rebuke with flames: “For by fire and by His sword, the LORD will execute judgment on all flesh, and many will be slain by the LORD.” The grove-consecrators, eating swine and vermin and rats, will perish together. And I, knowing their deeds and thoughts, “am coming to gather all nations and tongues, and they will come and see My glory”. A sign is set among them, and survivors are sent out as missionaries to the far map, Tarshish and Put and Lud and Tubal and Javan and the distant islands who have never heard His fame: “And they will bring all your brothers from all the nations as a gift to the LORD on horses and chariots and wagons, on mules and camels, to My holy mountain Jerusalem”, as Israel brings an offering in a clean vessel to the house of the LORD. “And I will select some of them as priests and Levites”: Gentiles in the priesthood, the eunuch's name and the foreigner's altar of chapter fifty-six arriving at their final office. “For just as the new heavens and the new earth, which I will make, will endure before Me”, “so your descendants and your name will endure”. “From one New Moon to another and from one Sabbath to another, all mankind will come to worship before Me”. And the book ends, deliberately, outside the gates, on the sight the worshipers pass on their way out: “As they go forth, they will see the corpses of the men who have rebelled against Me; for their worm will never die, their fire will never be quenched, and they will be a horror to all mankind.” No peace for the wicked was the refrain; the fire that never quenches is its last form. The book of the Holy One of Israel closes with worship in the center and horror at the perimeter, comfort promised and fulfilled, and the choice it opened with, scarlet or snow, extended to all flesh at the door. Isaiah said, Here am I, send me, in the year Uzziah died. Sixty-six chapters later, the sending is still going out, to Tarshish and the islands, and the last word of the book is not peace but a warning posted where everyone leaving worship will see it, exactly where the prophet would have wanted it: in plain sight, and impossible to unsee.
